articles.title: Nhóm “Con ghét bố mẹ” vượt 100.000 thành viên: Bên trong đang có gì?
articles.text:
Nhóm “Con ghét bố mẹ” đang viral trên mạng xã hội.
Mới đây, MXH xôn xao trước thông tin một hội nhóm có tên “Con ghét bố mẹ” bất ngờ thu hút lượng thành viên tăng chóng mặt. Hiện tại, đây là nhóm công khai, nghĩa là bất kỳ ai cũng có thể tìm thấy nhóm cũng như xem các nội dung được đăng tải tại đây.
Trên thực tế, nhóm này không phải mới xuất hiện. Theo thông tin hiển thị trên Facebook, “Con ghét bố mẹ” được lập từ năm 2021, với dòng giới thiệu: “Vào đây tâm sự bày tỏ những nỗi buồn trong gia đình khi bạn ghét bố mẹ”.
Tức là nhóm này đã tồn tại được khoảng 6 năm, song khoảng vài ngày trở lại đây bất ngờ viral, không rõ lý do, kéo theo lượng thành viên tăng nhanh.
Hồi tháng 4/2026, nhóm mới được ghi nhận ở quy mô hơn 2.100 thành viên. Tuy nhiên, chỉ trong thời gian ngắn trở lại đây, con số này liên tục tăng. Hôm qua, nhóm đã có hơn 40.000 thành viên. Đến 10h sáng nay (29/9) nhóm tiếp tục vượt mốc hơn 100.000 thành viên, cùng hơn 646 bài viết trong ngày. Con số này vẫn đang tiếp tục tăng.
Trong nhóm hơn 100.000 thành viên này có ai, đăng nội dung gì?
Theo tìm hiểu, thành viên trong nhóm này thuộc nhiều độ tuổi, tìm đến nhóm với nhiều mục đích khác nhau chứ không đơn thuần chỉ là những người ở vai “con”. Họ có thể là người đã trưởng thành, lập gia đình, đang có con nhỏ, người dùng MXH thấy tò mò nên join vào nhóm. Bài đăng trong nhóm công khai lẫn ẩn danh.
Nhiều bài đăng được viết bởi những tài khoản tự nhận là “con”, chia sẻ về những vấn đề trong gia đình. Nội dung vô vàn nhưng khó kiểm chứng sự thật, từ chuyện bố mẹ không hiểu mình, không được quan tâm, bị so sánh, áp lực học tập, chuyện tình cảm,... cho đến những mâu thuẫn trong sinh hoạt hằng ngày.
Ở phía các tài khoản nhận là phụ huynh, họ nhóm để trải lòng về chuyện làm cha mẹ, hoặc hỏi cách kết nối với con.
Có người dùng MXH cũng đến đây để chia sẻ góc nhìn với các bạn trẻ, phụ huynh.
Và, cũng có những người vào nhóm từ lâu nhưng đóng vai “tàu ngầm” để “hóng” thông tin.
Và đáng chú ý, có không ít tài khoản vào nhóm với mục đích đăng bài câu view, câu tương tác để bán hàng; đặc điểm nhận dạng của hội này là viết status mang màu sắc tiêu cực, tự nhận mình ở vai yếu thế bị đè nén về mặt cảm xúc, đưa ra những tình huống éo le đến sốc óc và trong phần comment thì… gắn link bán hàng!
Nhìn từ bên ngoài, “Con ghét bố mẹ” là một hội nhóm mở với số lượng thành viên đông đảo, ai cũng có thể tham gia. Tuy nhiên, xét về nội dung, đây lại là một không gian khó kiểm chứng thông tin, dễ kích thích sự tò mò, khơi lên cảm xúc tiêu cực và thậm chí điều hướng suy nghĩ, hành vi của người tham gia, thay vì đơn thuần là một group để mọi người chia sẻ và kết nối với nhau.
Không ai kiểm duyệt nội dung và hàng loạt nguy cơ phía sau
Một số người đặt vấn đề về quá trình kiểm duyệt và độ xác thực của những nội dung được chia sẻ trong nhóm “Con ghét bố mẹ”. Khi số lượng bài viết lên tới hàng trăm bài mỗi ngày, việc xác định đâu là câu chuyện có thật, đâu là nội dung được kể lại một chiều, thậm chí đâu là những bài viết được tạo ra với mục đích khác cũng không phải chuyện đơn giản.
Đặc biệt, những câu chuyện liên quan đến gia đình, mâu thuẫn giữa cha mẹ - con cái vốn rất dễ tác động đến cảm xúc người đọc. Một bài đăng kể về việc bị bố mẹ kiểm soát, không được thấu hiểu hay đối xử không công bằng có thể nhanh chóng nhận được sự đồng cảm từ hàng trăm, hàng nghìn người. Khi đó, cảm xúc của số đông cũng có thể trở thành yếu tố định hướng cách mọi người nhìn nhận câu chuyện, dù người đọc thực tế không biết đầy đủ hoàn cảnh của người đăng hay thiếu sự kiểm chứng cần thiết.
Bên cạnh những bài tâm sự, trong nhóm cũng xuất hiện những nội dung không hoàn toàn liên quan đến câu chuyện gia đình, trong đó có cả bài đăng gắn link bán hàng hoặc dẫn người dùng sang một nội dung khác. Điều này tiếp tục đặt ra câu hỏi: với một cộng đồng có lượng thành viên lớn và mức độ tương tác cao như vậy, liệu tất cả các bài đăng đang được chia sẻ đơn thuần vì nhu cầu tâm sự, hay một phần trong số đó có thể phục vụ những mục đích khác?
Ngay cả cái tên “Con ghét bố mẹ” cũng là một chi tiết đáng bàn.
Tên gọi này vốn đã mang sắc thái tiêu cực và phần nào tạo ra một “khung” để người dùng hình dung về cộng đồng trước cả khi đọc bài viết bên trong. Một người bước vào nhóm vì tò mò về những câu chuyện “ghét bố mẹ” có thể vô thức chú ý nhiều hơn đến các nội dung tiêu cực, những mâu thuẫn gay gắt hay trải nghiệm tổn thương. Từ đó, chính tên gọi cũng có thể ảnh hưởng đến cách người đọc tiếp nhận những câu chuyện xuất hiện trong nhóm. Khi người dùng đã bước vào với một chiếc “khung” có sẵn, liệu họ còn nhìn những mâu thuẫn cha mẹ - con cái hoàn toàn theo cách thấu hiểu?
Một vấn đề khác cũng bắt đầu được quan tâm khi nhóm tăng thành viên với tốc độ chóng mặt: giá trị của chính cộng đồng mà nhóm đang sở hữu.
Bởi khi một hội nhóm đạt quy mô hàng chục nghìn, thậm chí hàng trăm nghìn thành viên, nó không còn đơn thuần là nơi tập hợp những người có chung một mối quan tâm. Số lượng thành viên, lượt xem, bài đăng và tương tác tích lũy theo thời gian cũng tạo nên một tài sản số có giá trị nhất định.
Trên thực tế, một hội nhóm lớn có thể tiếp tục được duy trì theo mục đích ban đầu, thay đổi chủ đề, đổi cách vận hành hoặc được sử dụng cho những mục đích thương mại khác. Vì vậy, với một nhóm đang tăng trưởng thành viên rất nhanh, câu hỏi không chỉ nằm ở việc hôm nay mọi người đang nói gì trong đó, mà còn là: Cộng đồng này sẽ được sử dụng như thế nào khi đã đạt đến một quy mô đủ lớn?
Ở thời điểm hiện tại, khi “Con ghét bố mẹ” đã vượt mốc 100N thành viên, những câu hỏi về tính xác thực của nội dung, cách thức kiểm duyệt, khả năng tác động đến cảm xúc đám đông và mục đích vận hành lâu dài của nhóm cũng vì thế trở nên đáng chú ý hơn.

articles.title: Airbnb is adding a personalized map and other discovery tools - Engadget
articles.text:
Airbnb is adding a personalized map and other discovery tools
The rental service is getting more social and more AI.
Airbnb has announced a sweeping array of product features coming to the service as part of its fall update. The platform is adding a new social angle, allowing users to see where people they know have stayed on past travels. Airbnb will let people set their own privacy preferences about whether a trip is shared with others and how much detail is provided about that journey. Connections can view each others' past and upcoming trips, while a new Travel Map lets you browse their rentals as well as the services and experiences they booked through Airbnb. The update will also let you read reviews left by your social network and add their favorites to your own wishlists. You'll also be able to message connections within Airbnb's app.
The new interactive maps can also reveal neighborhood summaries, displaying an overview of an area based on data provided by guests and hosts. The post from Airbnb said these summaries would also include insights from "other sources," but did not elaborate on what that external information might be.
As you might expect, there are also new AI tools coming to the service in search, filters, listing descriptions, listing comparisons and customer support. Most of the new features are rolling out in the US now, though the AI-powered comparison tool will arrive later this year.
The Airbnb Services section of the app is continuing to build on the additions it introduced this spring. In Europe, users will soon see options for meal and grocery delivery. US users in select cities will be able to order quick-turnaround laundry services through Rinse or baby gear rentals via BabyQuip to their temporary lodgings. Airbnb is also partnering to offer more local activity bookings specific to certain locations, such as rentals for boats in South Florida or ski and snowboard gear in the French Alps.
Update, September 30, 2026, 12PM ET: This story was updated with additional details on the timeline for the AI-powered comparison tool.

articles.title: OpenAI's Jev clone could help the frontier lab stop its swarming agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
One of the more intriguing announcements at OpenAI’s Dev Day event on Tuesday came in an aside from CEO Sam Altman, who revealed the company’s new “Decisions API.”
The API apparently provides similar functionality to Jev, a model released by TypeSafe AI earlier this month that’s explicitly designed for software automation. A kind of super-powered classifier built on an LLM, developers can give Jev a set of choices that it outputs as probabilities cheaply and at high speeds.
OpenAI’s Decisions API seems to be the same sort of product. At the event, Altman described the API as a way to give the lab’s Luna model a predefined set of options to choose between, such as categories in which to classify an image or different agent behaviors.
“By focusing the model on that choice, we can make it extremely fast while keeping capabilities like image understanding, broad language support, and safety protections,” Altman said.
TypeSafe didn’t respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the new product, but CEO Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI engineer who co-invented reinforcement learning, joked on X about the beginning of the clone wars.
He added that OpenAI’s interest could be “a sign…that building in a System One compatible way is the future.” (“System One” is TypeSafe’s term of art for fast, intuitive thinking, versus “System 2,” which it applies to deliberate reasoning.)
The subtext here is that LLMs as we know them aren’t the right solution for a lot of software because they are comparatively slow and expensive. Developers have been using Jev to augment LLMs and, in doing so, have found that they’re faster and cheaper.
It’s not clear how similar Decisions API will be to Jev, since OpenAI released it as a limited preview and, thus far, TechCrunch hasn’t spotted developers running it through its paces. However, there is clearly interest, according to the conversations on X.
Decisions API isn’t the only Jev-like API on the internet — other startups are rolling out similar models; OpenAI won’t be the last tech giant to produce one. A key question is how well calibrated each of these decision models’ outputs will be to real life.
Almeida says his company’s moat is the synthetic data it creates to generate statistically useful outputs.
“Fast and cheap is very easy, you know,” Almeida told TechCrunch last week. “If you want it really fast and cheap, use dice, right? Intelligence is the hard part, and my North Star is always pushing the intelligence-per-dollar Pareto curve.”
After just weeks, it seems clear that these models have a future ahead of them, and one likely application is monitoring and securing AI agents. One of OpenAI’s new security measures following a series of incidents where its agents misbehaved on the open internet is using a separate model to watch for bad actions at “significant compute cost.”
Shapor Naghibzadeh, a long-time cybersecurity professional who leads the startup QueryStory, thinks that a model like Jev could make that possible far more cheaply.
He built a demo for a hackathon held last weekend that uses Jev to check each agentic action against the task it was given, blocking actions it had high confidence were bad, flagging others for review, and permitting the rest.
In theory, such monitoring could have stopped the Hugging Face incident — and monitoring of that kind costs $2.94 with Jev, versus $372 with a frontier LLM.
A key observation is that Jev is arguably cheap enough to run on every agentic action, which offers a layer of review that could improve the reliability of agents writ large. It’s the kind of thing TypeSafe was hoping to achieve — and now OpenAI has seen the value as well.

articles.title: How Israeli Checkpoints Choke Palestinian Life in the Occupied West Bank
articles.text:
How Israeli checkpoints suffocate Palestinian life in the occupied West Bank.
Illustration: Hokyoung Kim
The Big Story
Sep 30, 2026 6:00 AM
Lama Rabah
Sabrina Slipchenko
Charles Boutaud
Firas Tawil
Elena DeBre
Choke Points
Lost time. Lost jobs. Lost friends. Lost family. Lost lives. How Israeli checkpoints suffocate Palestinian life in the occupied West Bank.
Illustration: Hokyoung Kim
The Big Story
Sep 30, 2026 6:00 AM
Lama Rabah
Sabrina Slipchenko
Charles Boutaud
Firas Tawil
Elena DeBre
Aref Jaber is on a neighbor's roof, trying to get home.
At 51, he is clambering over a wall into the next backyard, up onto the next roof, along the line of stone houses that stand between him and his own front door. He has no choice. Alleys and side streets in his neighborhood have been sealed with cement blocks and barbed wire, and a single point of access, called Checkpoint 160, is the only way in or out for the 140 families who live there.
But Checkpoint 160 is closed again; Jaber is not sure why. The whim of a soldier, a crash in the scanning system, breaking news in the region—it could be anything.
For the last three years, he says, this has happened at least two days a week. So the community has devised a system of alternative routes. Jaber calls his neighbors to ask if he can come through. They check their windows for soldiers, and then Jaber scales ladders and traverses roofs. “When I finally get home,” he says, “it feels like I’ve achieved something monumental.”
The enclosure of Jaber’s neighborhood is a dense microcosm of what life is becoming across the occupied West Bank—for Palestinians, that is. At the same time that deadly Israeli settler violence robs communities in the West Bank of their land, and amid the genocide in Gaza, Israel has expanded its infrastructures of military control and domination.
Since 2023, Israel’s fragmentation of Palestine, underway for generations, has accelerated. The West Bank has, for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians who live there, ceased to exist as a contiguous territory. According to the most recent UN data from December 2025, at least 925 fixed and temporary checkpoints, metal gates, roadblocks, and earth mounds divide the West Bank. (A Palestinian governmental commission reported this month that the number is now 942.) This fracturing has torn families apart, stifled the economy, and obstructed access to essential services such as hospitals and schools.
Aref Jaber climbs onto the roof of a neighbor's home to get to the street in the Jaber neighborhood in Hebron.PHOTOGRAPH: SAMAR HAZBOUN
Israel has never publicly listed the checkpoints it operates, their staffing hours, or their closure times. On the ground, Google Maps is practically useless for Palestinians; it is blind to the checkpoints and tries to route drivers onto roads reserved for Israeli-plated cars. Instead, citizens have developed their own ad hoc networks to inform each other of closures.
As far as we know, no organization has used that network—combined with new datasets and on-the-ground reporting—to measure what this does to daily life.
Over 18 months, WIRED, Lighthouse Reports, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism (ARIJ) and the Palestine Reporting Lab investigated the system that has carved the West Bank into cantons and measured what it cost people to move through it.
We analyzed tens of thousands of Telegram messages Palestinians sent to navigate daily checkpoint delays and closures
Working with the Institute for Social and Economic Progress (ISEP), a Palestinian research organization, we polled hundreds of people across the West Bank to find out how checkpoints shape their lives.

Then, we manually verified over 800 movement obstacles using satellite imagery and on-the-ground reporting, and we mapped 2.6 billion GPS pings of drivers navigating the roads and closures. Explore and download the full map of verified checkpoints here.

Obstacles in 2023
Obstacles added 2023-2025
The average West Bank commuter—someone who drives several times a week—loses about an hour and a half each week to additional travel time in an effort to avoid checkpoints. Over the course of a year, that amounts to 77 hours lost.
For some, the delays are far longer. People going from Ramallah to Al-Eizariya, on the edges of Jerusalem, could do so in 27 kilometers/48 minutes. Instead, it's 45 kilometers/100 minutes.
Our data shows that people have to take all sorts of complex routes to avoid checkpoints.
Using the median route taken in our dataset, someone who commutes back and forth four days a week would lose nearly seven hours in additional travel time every week.
Anyone who commutes four days a week from Ramallah to Hebron is robbed of over 12 extra hours of travel time.
One pair of towns, Anabta and Beit Lid, are 8 kilometers apart.
It used to be a 10 minute drive. It now routinely takes 50 minutes each way.
Our data analysis found that checkpoint delays have increased by more than 50 percent in the aftermath of October 2023, frequently exceeding hours at a time.
Together, Palestinians in the West Bank lose about 30 years every day.
Data can count the checkpoints, clock the closures, and tally the hours lost at the gates. But how does the system upend the life of a single family?
Losing Access to an Education
More than a decade ago, Amal and her family left the US. They moved back to a home in Al-Janiya, where they built a house with a garden, and a mountain view. “Mashallah,” she says of it still. (The names have been changed due to safety concerns.)
By the time the family arrived, Al-Janiya's main entrance had already been closed for over a decade. Israel sealed the eastern road in 2003; it now serves as an entrance to Talmon, an Israeli settlement built on the village's land.
The only way in or out of Al-Janiya that Amal's family has ever used runs west, through the neighboring village of Ras Karkar. Fifteen minutes down that road is her husband's shop in Ramallah.
A little further on, a local university, where her daughter Lina studies software engineering.
With open roads, Lina's commute could be around 12 kilometers/20 minutes.
With the detour because of a checkpoint, it became 32 kilometers/47 minutes.
Amal’s eldest, Dana, went farthest, to another university to study dentistry. She is set to be the first doctor in the family.
Dana's commute should be around 35.5 kilometers/47 minutes. It is now often a 90-minute drive.
AL JANIYA
RAS KARKAR
RAMALLAH
BIRZEIT UNIVERSITY
AL QUDS UNIVERSITY
Every day that Dana and Lina drive to their universities, they each lose about an hour on the circuitous route and at checkpoints. Over the course of an academic year, they have lost about three days each due to the detours.
“You loop and loop and end up at the same point… I swear, I get dizzy… By the time you arrive, you're just sad. You sit there asking yourself: what is this life?” Amal said. "You can take it once. Twice. For a year. Then it crosses some limit and you can’t.”
Thirty percent of people in the West Bank said that checkpoints have prevented them from starting or completing a university education. Most students living outside major cities cross at least one checkpoint on the shortest route to their nearest university.
Last summer, Amal's family decided they couldn’t spend another academic year in Al-Janiya, and they moved near Ramallah. “We grieve leaving our village,” Amal said, “but it’s not really a choice.”
They join more than one in ten people in the West Bank who say they’ve moved to other cities or regions because of checkpoints, along with 31 percent who say they’re considering moving for the same reason.
An Inheritance of Loss
Roads that once tied Palestine together have been closed off again and again, first by militarized borders and barriers, then by permits, and finally by hundreds of checkpoints.
Khalil Tufakji, a Palestinian cartographer and expert on Israeli settlements, has watched Israel assemble this system for decades. The purpose of checkpoints is the fragmentation of space, he said—“every city closes in on itself”—and in this way, the homeland shrinks to a city.
The system that confines Palestinians was built in layers. Under British colonial rule, Palestinian communities were at times subjected to roadblocks, systemic and capricious searches, border barriers, and a system of permits that restricted who could move by vehicle across the territory.
In 1948, in what is known as the “Nakba” or “catastrophe,” Zionist forces expelled more than 750,000 Palestinians from their homes. Hundreds of villages were depopulated or destroyed, and people were driven into exile.
Those who remained were placed under Israeli military rule for the next 18 years, forbidden to work, trade, study, or seek medical care beyond their towns without an Israeli permit.
In 1967, when Israel seized the remaining Palestinian territories, it reconstructed the same permit system there. Palestinians were sorted into categories, the color of an ID card determining who may go where.
In 1988, UN Special Committee reports classified the closing of areas in the occupied territories as collective punishment.
In 1995, the Oslo Process resumed. It was meant to lead to the establishment of a sovereign Palestinian state. Instead, it further fragmented Palestinians by dividing the West Bank into administrative islands.
By the early 2000s, this system of closures and permits had become the status quo. In 2002, Israel started building the 713-kilometers-long separation wall, 85 percent of which runs through the West Bank.
And since 2007, Israel has imposed a blockade on Gaza, isolating it from the rest of Palestine.
In the years that followed, the restrictions intensified.

This has meant that every generation of Palestinians since 1948 has inherited a smaller world than the one before it. Grandparents in Jenin, a city in the northern West Bank, tell stories about driving to have lunch in Jerusalem or a weekend in Beirut.
Parents from West Bank towns mention visiting Gaza. Their children remember school trips to Jericho's ancient sites, to an amusement park in Tulkarm and to the zoo in Qalqilya. Most people in the West Bank today have never been to Gaza, according to the ISEP poll. Over 40 percent of respondents said they had never seen the sea, though from high points, in places like Ramallah, you can see it in the distance.
A Palestinian family on the beach of Gaza on August 25, 1997.PHOTOGRAPH: ANTOINE GYORI/GETTY IMAGES
Today, people in the West Bank are living through another period of fragmentation. Three-quarters of those living in the West Bank have close relatives in other governorates. A quarter of parents said their children have never met close relatives who live in other parts of the West Bank. A generation is being locked in: Nearly a third of people under the age of 25 say they’ve never even left their own governorate.
In response to WIRED’s questions, the Israeli Military said, “Decisions regarding the placement of roadblocks, their opening or closing, are made in accordance with operational situation assessments and security considerations alone.” It is a policy that is “continuously adjusted according to the situational assessment on the ground, while balancing the residents’ ability to move freely throughout the area and security needs.”
In a letter addressed to Israel’s Central Command and top military officials, as reported by the newspaper Haaretz in June, the legal adviser to the Israeli military, Colonel Cobi Marcus, advised that the current system of checkpoints and movement obstacles has intensified beyond any legal justification. Haaretz reported he “warned” that since October 2023, the proliferation of movement restrictions, imposed on residents without authorization, may violate basic rights and the principles of international law.
Rema Hammami, an anthropologist at Birzeit University who has researched checkpoints, calls the current situation unprecedented. “Every single community, village, every single Palestinian city is going to be a separate prison. And if there's no pushback on it, they’re just going to keep going forward with it.”
There have been military checkpoints in other parts of the world, like Sri Lanka and Iraq. But Hammami says nowhere compares to the "density, scope, and comprehensiveness” of the system in the West Bank.
A Family Split
Route 60 was part of Reem Yassin’s life for six years. It’s the West Bank's central highway and the main road connecting Ramallah, the West Bank’s political hub, with Nablus, the commercial center of the north.
Yassin was the senior resident anesthesiologist at An-Najah National University Hospital, a leading medical facility in Nablus, which is 45 kilometers away from her home in Ramallah, in the central West Bank.
Yassin says the drive took her around 40 minutes in 2020, when she began her residency—an annoying but manageable commute. After October 2023, the Israeli military erected an additional three checkpoints on the most direct route between Ramallah and Nablus, and she says existing checkpoints began to close far more frequently.
When she gave birth to her first daughter, Yara, she would drop the baby off at her parents house in ’Asirah al-Qibliyah, a village south of Nablus, which meant she had to pass through a different checkpoint, Al-Muraba’ah, off Route 60.
Data analysis shows that since October 2023, Al-Muraba’ah has been one of the most congested checkpoints in the West Bank, often becoming a chokepoint as other routes into Nablus were closed. It would routinely take drivers 20 to 30 minutes to cross, but delays of several hours weren’t uncommon.
To make it work, Yassin would pack the night before, like she was catching a long flight: snacks, a breast pump, clothes for herself and for Yara. She would leave the Ramallah apartment in the dark, before 6 am, to drop Yara in 'Asirah before crossing Al-Muraba’ah.
"I didn't have a life anymore," she says. "I’d go to work and see my daughter for an hour at night. The rest of the time was at the checkpoint." She is one of a third of West Bank parents who say that checkpoints regularly prevent them from seeing their children during their waking hours.
The patterns are unpredictable. One moment, cars pass the checkpoint without much delay; at another, it can take hours. Events that should have little bearing on West Bank mobility can suddenly trigger a lockdown. On June 13 and 14, 2025, when Israel began bombing Iran, about 70 percent of checkpoints were suddenly closed, according to our analysis of Telegram data, an almost 350 percent increase from the week before.
Alexandra Rijke, a cultural geographer who spent years researching checkpoints in the West Bank, calls unpredictability one of the occupation's core mechanisms. Not knowing whether you can go to work or school, or what will get you punished, has a huge impact on people's lives. "Arbitrariness is incredibly violent," she said.
Across the West Bank, the roads between whole regions converge at a handful of checkpoints.
Their closure can divide north from south, force drivers away from their destination before they can turn back toward it, and leave an entire city dependent on a few guarded exits.
The Divide
Every journey we mapped from the southern West Bank toward the center and north narrowed to Wadi an-Nar.
The Divide
When its gates close, it cuts the West Bank in two.
The Detour
The fastest road from Ramallah toward East Jerusalem and the southern West Bank passes through Jaba checkpoint.
The Detour
When it closes, often to give settlers an open road on the other side, drivers must head north before they can turn east and south again.
The Enclosure
Qalqilya city reaches the rest of the West Bank through only a few roads.
The Enclosure
When the main entrance closes, drivers are forced south before they can turn back east.
The Enclosure
Close the remaining access road and a city of 60,000 is left all but sealed off.
RAMALLAH
BETHLEHEM

Yassin follows a protocol for crossing. Windows down before the soldiers ask. Then the script, which she can recite: "Hand over your ID. Where are you going, where are you coming from, what do you do?" Sometimes the soldier holds his phone up close and takes photos of her face with her ID and license plate. One time, she said, a soldier leaned in through the window: "You're beautiful," he said.
She often saw men pressed face-down against the hoods of their cars, hands behind their backs, the soldiers shouting. Sometimes, on her way back, the same men are still detained.
When asked, nearly two-thirds of people say humiliation or fear most characterize their feeling about checkpoints. Of people stopped at a checkpoint in the last six months, nearly 40 percent said their vehicle was searched by a soldier, and more than 20 percent said they were physically searched. About one in seven said a soldier had pointed a gun toward them.
Eventually, even dropping her daughter off in the morning stopped making sense. Yassin began staying at her parents' house near Nablus most nights. Her husband Montasir stayed in Ramallah and visited on some weekends. He usually left them Saturday morning, before the settler traffic on Route 60 picked up and checkpoints got worse.
As Yara grew older, she began to ask questions. When she opened her eyes in the morning, she’d ask: "Mama, why didn't you take us to Baba?" Then, because she already knew the answer, she’d say, "Is the road closed?"
In the end, the checkpoints proved too great a barrier for Yassin too. The move to her parents’ wasn’t enough. She was still losing hours at the checkpoint. After her second child was born earlier this year, Yassin decided not to go back to work. She extended her maternity leave and was weighing what comes next: a pause, a position closer to home if she can find one, perhaps something abroad. "I can't do it again," she said. Since then, Yassin has left her job at the hospital.
Deadly Delays
In the summer of July 2024, a young man from Reem Yassin’s village was shot by Israeli forces in the leg. The injury itself was not life threatening. But after soldiers held his ambulance at a checkpoint for almost an hour, he entered severe hemorrhagic shock, Yassin recalled.
Yassin, who was completing part of her medical residency at Rafidia Surgical Hospital in Nablus, was the doctor who received him. Recognized immediately by his family, she worked to stabilize him as his blood pressure plunged.
"We almost lost him," Yassin recalls. "We had to keep pumping blood into him." He survived, luckily, but his situation is far from unique: Nearly two-thirds of people in the West Bank say checkpoints have been a barrier to their access to medical care.
Between October 2023 and August 2026, the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) documented 237 access denials and 240 mission delays by Israeli forces. In early 2026, incidents included soldiers detaining a medical crew at the Sarra checkpoint, soldiers throwing an ambulance crew’s keys down a mountainside at Huwwara, and a Palestinian woman in labor being transferred between vehicles across locked gates. (In response to questions on medical delays, the Israeli Military said, “In accordance with international law, the IDF allows freedom of movement for medical vehicles, including ambulances, for the purpose of providing medical treatment and evacuating the wounded.”)
These delays carry fatal consequences. The Red Crescent attributes 25 deaths since 2023 to the obstruction of its medical teams. In July 2026, a Palestinian infant, Ahmad Zaid, died after Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint blocked the vehicle transporting him for more than an hour.
In response, the Red Crescent has begun bringing facilities to the people, building makeshift medical points inside villages since ambulances are now so often delayed and cannot reliably access hospitals. Doctors Without Borders (MSF) also started providing first aid training to medical and nonmedical volunteers so they can respond to urgent medical needs in cases when an ambulance is delayed or stopped at a checkpoint.
Sleeping at the Factory
After October 2023, delay times at checkpoints across Nablus spiked to levels beyond anywhere else in the West Bank. Commuters in Nablus spent an average of nearly an hour and 50 minutes avoiding checkpoints. Ali Haj Ali has worked at Sama Pharmaceuticals, a medicine factory east of Nablus city, for over a decade; now, at 37, he supervises the maintenance of the company’s production lines. When he leaves at the end of his shift at 4:30 pm, he has stopped expecting to reach his home before 8:00 pm, even though it’s only 16 kilometers away.
Some nights, he doesn't get home at all. He sleeps at the factory, in an arrangement Sama built during Covid-19: Two offices hold a bed and a dozen mattresses for whoever can’t make the trip home.
When checkpoints close, Sama’s employees sometimes have to sleep on site.PHOTOGRAPH: Lama Rabah
“My three kids, my wife, my mother, my father, I’d barely see them,” he said. “And forget about seeing friends.” But this is the best job he thinks he can find, so he keeps going.
On a recent afternoon, Ali sat in a room at Sama Pharmaceuticals, along with his colleague, Ohood Khatatbeh. In minutes, they were filling in the details for one another, recounting what they call “Nablus’ checkpoint crisis” in 2024 and 2025. Ali would sometimes reach the checkpoint, sit there for hours, then just turn around and go home.
"Nothing is guaranteed, that's just how it is here. It's like a lottery," Ali said.
Ohood, the factory’s quality assurance manager, is 38 years old, and the mother of three sons. Her town, Beit Furik, is southeast of Nablus. It has a single gate, in or out. Her whole day is dictated by that gate.
The town has had to come up with its own protocol, as Ohood calls it: For every three private cars, one shared taxi gets through. What they cannot control is the pace, interrupted by the soldiers’ change of shifts.
Best case, if the Beit Furik gate is open and traffic is moving freely, the drive home can take 15 minutes. But for a year and a half, it routinely took her more than 5 hours daily. On the worst day, it took 10 hours. In 2024, Ohood's teenage son had finished a final exam in biology at his school in Nablus just before she was finishing her shift. They found each other at the Beit Furik gate at 4:30 pm, in a line that packed the road several cars wide, all heading for the single entrance to a town of almost 16,000.
Ohood and her son waited in line together until 3 am the following morning.
"The regular employee, the one not separated from work by a checkpoint," she said, "would be home, eaten, showered, asleep, and already dreaming, while I'm still at the checkpoint."
Across the West Bank, checkpoints have begun to reshape how businesses like Sama operate. The company has started rejecting highly qualified candidates after assessing the checkpoints they would have to cross to get to work, Ohood said. It’s even started writing it into the job postings, as a requirement: Candidates must live in Nablus. About half of people polled said checkpoints have impacted their or their spouse’s ability to get a job.
In late 2025, Ohood’s one-week-old baby, Aws, came down with jaundice. She and her husband drove him out of town to the hospital. But on the way back, as she remembers it, they found the soldier already closing the gate.
"Go back," the soldier yelled in Arabic from the other side of the gate in Beit Furik.
"Go back where?" her husband asked. "We have a sick child with us."
The soldier raised his rifle and pointed it toward them. "For God's sake," Ohood told her husband, "let's just go back." He tried once more anyway, offering to turn around himself if the soldier would just let Ohood and the baby cross the gate on foot. The soldier lost his temper. "I'll shoot you," he said.
They turned around, the baby crying in their arms, and waited in line for an hour and a half until the soldier opened the gate again.
A Different World
By 2000, Aref Jaber says every road in and out of the Jaber neighborhood in Hebron, named after his family, was sealed with earth mounds and concrete slabs. By 2010, he says, iron gates were installed and checkpoints were manned by soldiers. Three years ago, new closures were installed on the very entrances to people's homes, and iron fencing was wrapped around the gates so no one could squeeze through.
The neighborhood sits between the Ibrahimi Mosque, the settlement outposts in the old city in Hebron, and the Kiryat Arba settlement, and has only one way in or out: a turnstile, an inspection room with digital scanning, a metal gate, and a military watchtower, called Checkpoint 160. It’s “as if we’re entering another country,” Jaber says of crossing it. Except the country on the other side is his own house.
For months after October 2023, Israeli forces imposed a curfew on the neighborhood every night, from 10 to 7 in the morning. Now it's every weekend, Aref said. From Friday afternoon until Sunday morning, the checkpoint is closed. No one in, no one out. Jaber says the people who die on Sundays are lucky, because you can bury them the same day. Die on a Saturday, and there is nothing to be done until the checkpoint opens again.
The Palestinians in the neighborhood need to wait for Israeli approval for things big and small: whether they want to evacuate a patient, hold a funeral, or bring in a canister of cooking gas. Locals cross the checkpoint on foot and climb the hill, carrying the sick, carrying groceries up to the neighborhood, dragging suitcases down toward the checkpoint. Jaber’s 6-year-old grandson should be able to go to the school 50 meters away. But it now sits behind an earth mound wrapped in barbed wire, and reaching it would mean a three-kilometer detour on foot, along settler-dominated roads. Jaber waves at his cousins, who live behind the same earth mound. "They have a whole different life there," he says. "We're in the closed zone."
Houses belonging to Palestinians who have been forced to leave them or use a different entrance by the Israeli Military and Israeli settlers are seen in the Jaber neighborhood of Hebron.PHOTOGRAPH: SAMAR HAZBOUN
Even amid the unrelenting pressure of apartheid, people can still imagine a different life. On January 6, 2026, at around 3:00 pm, a Palestinian driver approached Wadi an-Nar, the checkpoint controlling the only road linking the north of the occupied West Bank to the south since 2000. He noticed something strange. No soldiers stood in the way. The checkpoint was open. He took out his phone, recorded a twenty-second video, and posted it in a local Telegram channel.
Within the hour, the clip spread through the West Bank. Everyone was confused. Did Israel remove its checkpoints? Was this really happening?
At 5:57, admins of the “Road Conditions” Telegram group were joking about crossing checkpoints off their lists.
At 6:10, the admins posted that the soldiers had returned. At 6:12, they said the gates were shut.
There was never an explanation. Some assumed it was a drill for Israeli forces. Others, simply a change of shifts. But for three hours, people allowed themselves to imagine a West Bank without checkpoints. A West Bank you can drive the full length of, 130 kilometers from north to south, in less than two hours.
And for a moment, they inhabited a world where they could plan the next day, the next hour. Where Amal’s daughters would reach their lecture halls in minutes. Where Reem wouldn't have to give up a job to keep her family together. Where Ali would walk through his front door before his son fell asleep. Where Ohood would take her baby to the hospital without a rifle raised at her. Where, perhaps, you just keep driving: to Haifa, to Gaza, anywhere you want.
And Aref Jaber would walk down his own street, past the ladders he no longer needs. He would open his front door, and be home.

articles.title: Apple Pay finally arrives in India on a limited basis - Engadget
articles.text:
Apple Pay finally arrives in India on a limited basis
It only supports Axis Bank cards for now.
Apple Pay has arrived in India, making the contactless payment service available to the world's most populated country. It took Apple over a decade since the feature's inception to be able to roll it out to the market, because it had to comply with local banking regulations.
For now, however, the feature only supports Visa and MasterCard credit cards issued by Axis Bank. It still doesn't work with cards issued by other banks in the country, such as the State Bank of India and HDFC Bank. And as TechCrunch notes, it doesn't support India's local credit card network RuPay. The publication says Apple wants to charge a 0.2 percent fee per transaction, and its terms are still under negotiation with the other banks.
In addition, it will not work on terminals that haven't been enabled for the payment method. The company did say in its announcement that "millions of merchants across India" will accept Apple Pay at launch, including "Apple Store locations, Blinkit, Chaayos, Comet, Croma, Interflora, Ixigo, Le15 Patisserie, Reliance brands, Tata 1mg, Zomato and more."
Like in other regions, users in India can add Axis Bank cards through the bank's app or via tapping the plus sign inside the Wallet app and following instructions. India's smartphone market is still dominated by Android phones, but Counterpoint Research told CNBC that Apple's volume market share is likely to reach 10 percent this year, thanks to the strong demand for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

articles.title: Long Châu và hành trình xây dựng niềm tin từ những điều người Việt cần
articles.text:
Từ một hệ thống nhà thuốc, Long Châu đang mở rộng “hệ sinh thái” bằng cách kết hợp mạng lưới, đội ngũ dược sĩ, dịch vụ chăm sóc sức khỏe và công nghệ.
Luôn có mặt khi người dân cần: Long Châu và mạng lưới chăm sóc sức khỏe rộng khắp
Với những sản phẩm, dịch vụ liên quan đến sức khỏe, khả năng tiếp cận là một yếu tố quan trọng. Một thương hiệu có sản phẩm phù hợp nhưng không dễ tìm thấy khi cần sẽ khó trở thành lựa chọn quen thuộc trong đời sống hàng ngày.
Long Châu hiện sở hữu hơn 2.700 nhà thuốc và khoảng 240 trung tâm tiêm chủng trên toàn quốc, tạo mạng lưới để người dân tiếp cận thuốc và các dịch vụ chăm sóc sức khỏe thuận tiện hơn.
Tuy nhiên, mở rộng mạng lưới chỉ là một phần của bài toán. Với người dùng, niềm tin còn đến từ những yếu tố cụ thể: sản phẩm có nguồn gốc rõ ràng, giá được niêm yết minh bạch và có dược sĩ trực tiếp tư vấn. Hệ thống nhà thuốc đạt chuẩn GPP cùng tiêu chí phục vụ “đúng thuốc, đúng liều, đúng cách và đúng giá” là những yếu tố được Long Châu xây dựng trong quá trình vận hành.
Theo cách này, niềm tin bắt đầu từ những trải nghiệm rất cơ bản khi cần thuốc, có một địa chỉ để tìm đến; khi có thắc mắc, có người có chuyên môn để hỏi; khi lựa chọn sản phẩm, có thông tin để kiểm chứng.
Hiểu người dùng hơn: Khi công nghệ trở thành công cụ xây dựng niềm tin
Khi hành vi chăm sóc sức khỏe ngày càng dịch chuyển lên môi trường số, sự thuận tiện cũng trở thành một phần trong kỳ vọng của người dùng. Công nghệ vì thế đang mở rộng cách thương hiệu đồng hành với khách hàng, từ cung cấp sản phẩm đến hỗ trợ nhiều nhu cầu trong quá trình chăm sóc sức khỏe.
Công nghệ cũng được đưa vào những nhu cầu đời thường của gia đình. AI Kể chuyện bằng giọng của mẹ sử dụng AI tạo sinh giọng nói để tạo trải nghiệm kể chuyện cho trẻ; OCR và thị giác máy tính hỗ trợ trích xuất thông tin từ phiếu khám; mô hình 3D mô phỏng quá trình phát triển của thai nhi theo từng tuần.
Trong khi đó, Sổ tiêm chủng điện tử kết nối hồ sơ trẻ với hệ thống Trung tâm Tiêm chủng Long Châu, giúp dữ liệu được đồng bộ thuận tiện hơn.
Điểm đáng chú ý là công nghệ không nhằm thay thế đội ngũ chuyên môn. Dữ liệu và AI có thể hỗ trợ cha mẹ theo dõi, quản lý thông tin và tiếp cận dịch vụ, trong khi những vấn đề cần đánh giá chuyên môn vẫn cần đến bác sĩ, dược sĩ hoặc chuyên gia phù hợp.
Theo hướng đó, công nghệ trở thành công cụ giúp thông tin và dịch vụ đến gần người dùng hơn, đồng thời tạo ra trải nghiệm nhất quán trong quá trình chăm sóc sức khỏe.
Từ nơi bán thuốc đến người đồng hành trong hành trình chăm sóc sức khỏe
Khi nhu cầu của người dân không dừng lại ở việc mua thuốc, vai trò của một hệ thống bán lẻ dược phẩm cũng có thể mở rộng theo hướng chăm sóc sức khỏe chủ động hơn.
Với Long Châu, mạng lưới nhà thuốc là nền tảng để tiếp cận người dùng; đội ngũ dược sĩ vững chuyên môn; hệ thống trung tâm tiêm chủng mở rộng các dịch vụ chăm sóc sức khỏe dự phòng; còn công nghệ giúp kết nối thông tin và nâng cao sự thuận tiện trong chăm sóc sức khỏe hàng ngày.
Bên cạnh hoạt động kinh doanh, Long Châu cũng phối hợp với chính quyền địa phương, các đơn vị y tế triển khai nhiều chương trình khám bệnh, tầm soát sức khỏe và cấp phát thuốc miễn phí khắp các vùng miền. Hành trình này hướng tới việc đưa các hoạt động chăm sóc sức khỏe đến gần hơn với người dân, nâng cao sức khỏe cộng đồng.
Nhìn từ hành trình đó, niềm tin không đến từ một sản phẩm, một điểm bán hay một chiến dịch riêng lẻ mà được tích lũy qua nhiều lần người dùng tìm đến thương hiệu: Khi cần mua thuốc, tiêm chủng; cần được tư vấn cùng các chuyên gia y tế; theo dõi sức khỏe của gia đình qua nền tảng trực tuyến…
Từ những nhu cầu rất cơ bản ấy, Long Châu đang kết hợp mạng lưới, chuyên môn dược sĩ, dịch vụ chăm sóc sức khỏe và công nghệ để mở rộng vai trò “điểm tựa” sức khỏe trong đời sống người Việt. Niềm tin, sau cùng, được hình thành từ chính những trải nghiệm mà người dùng có thể cảm nhận và kiểm chứng qua thời gian.

articles.title: Lãi suất ngân hàng hôm nay 30/9/2026: Chứng chỉ tiền gửi Big4 cao nhất 7,5%/năm
articles.text:
Áp lực cân đối nguồn vốn, đặc biệt là vốn cho vay trung và dài hạn, khiến các ngân hàng tích cực phát hành chứng chỉ tiền gửi để thu hút nguồn vốn.
Chứng chỉ tiền gửi thường được các ngân hàng trả lãi suất cao hơn từ 1-3 điểm phần trăm so với lãi suất huy động thông thường. Tại một số ngân hàng thương mại cổ phần, lãi suất huy động chứng chỉ tiền gửi cao nhất lên đến 9,4%/năm.
Trong khi đó, nhóm ngân hàng thương mại nhà nước như Vietcombank, VietinBank, BIDV, lãi suất chứng chỉ tiền gửi cao nhất là 7,5%/năm, vượt trội so với lãi suất tiết kiệm truyền thống được nhóm Big4 niêm yết.
Cụ thể, Vietcombank niêm yết lãi suất chứng chỉ tiền gửi kỳ hạn 6 tháng là 7,5%/năm. Sản phẩm có mệnh giá 100.000 đồng, số lượng mua tối thiểu 200 chứng chỉ và phải là bội số của 10.
Theo quy định của ngân hàng, giao dịch mua chứng chỉ tiền gửi được phục vụ từ 6h đến 21h các ngày làm việc. Giao dịch chuyển quyền sở hữu theo hình thức mua, bán với Vietcombank được thực hiện từ 9h đến 15h cùng ngày.
Hiện Vietcombank chỉ niêm yết lãi suất chứng chỉ tiền gửi với duy nhất kỳ hạn 6 tháng.
Tại BIDV, lãi suất chứng chỉ tiền gửi được niêm yết cho các kỳ hạn từ 1-60 tháng.
Lãi suất chứng chỉ tiền gửi kỳ hạn 1-5 tháng là 4,75%/năm, tương đương lãi suất tiền gửi trực tuyến thông thường. Với các kỳ hạn 6-11 tháng và 13-60 tháng, mức lãi suất được niêm yết là 7,2%/năm.
Lãi suất cao nhất được BIDV niêm yết cho chứng chỉ tiền gửi kỳ hạn 12 tháng là 7,4%/năm.
Tương tự BIDV, VietinBank niêm yết lãi suất chứng chỉ tiền gửi kỳ hạn 1-5 tháng ở mức 4,75%/năm. Các kỳ hạn 6-9 tháng có lãi suất 7,2%/năm, trong khi kỳ hạn 12-36 tháng được áp dụng mức 7,4%/năm.
Theo TS. Nguyễn Văn Lộc, Giám đốc Chương trình đào tạo Kinh doanh thương mại, Đại học Phenikaa, việc các ngân hàng đồng thời đẩy mạnh phát hành chứng chỉ tiền gửi cho thấy nhu cầu bổ sung nguồn vốn trung, dài hạn ngày càng cấp thiết.
Ông Lộc nhận định, trong bối cảnh tăng trưởng tín dụng được duy trì ở mức cao, các công cụ huy động vốn ngoài tiền gửi truyền thống sẽ tiếp tục đóng vai trò quan trọng. Tuy nhiên, điều này cũng đồng nghĩa chi phí vốn của hệ thống ngân hàng có xu hướng gia tăng trong thời gian tới.

articles.title: AI voice startup ElevenLabs doubles valuation to $22B | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Voice AI startup ElevenLabs announced today that it’s allowing employees to cash out a portion of their vested equity at a $22 billion valuation, doubling the $11 billion valuation the company hit when it raised $500 million in February.
The recent $300 million tender offer gave employees an opportunity to sell their shares to investors. The transaction was co-led by Wellington and T. Rowe Price, large institutional investors that back private companies with the intention of retaining the stock after the company goes public.
The offering is part of a growing trend among fast-growing AI startups that use employee liquidity as a retention tool to prevent staff from leaving for competitors.
This is the second time that four-year-old ElevenLabs has authorized a secondary transaction for employees. The company previously held a $100 million tender at a $6.6 billion valuation in September 2025.
Founded in 2022, the company is known for generating ultra-realistic human voices and sound effects. With its new valuation, New York- and London-based ElevenLabs joins the ranks of Europe’s most valuable startups.
TechCrunch sat down with co-founder and CEO Mati Staniszewski last week.

articles.title: Xe nhập giảm giá 90 triệu: Công nghiệp phụ trợ mất đi những gì?
articles.text:
Khi chuyển sang nhập từ Thái Lan, BYD Dolphin giảm giá khởi điểm 90 triệu đồng. Người mua được lợi thật, nhưng khoản rẻ ấy đổi lấy những thứ không hiện trên bảng giá, gồm đơn hàng linh kiện, việc làm trong nhà máy và nguồn thu ngân sách.
Khoản lợi có thật
Tháng 4 năm nay, BYD đưa mẫu Dolphin về Việt Nam từ nhà máy tại Thái Lan thay vì từ Trung Quốc. Giá khởi điểm giảm từ 659 triệu xuống 569 triệu đồng. Lý do nằm ở thuế, khi xe con xuất xứ Trung Quốc chịu thuế nhập khẩu 50%, còn xe sản xuất tại các nước ASEAN được hưởng 0%.
Người mua hưởng lợi trực tiếp từ chênh lệch này. VCCI từng cho rằng các rào cản hiện nay đang giữ giá xe tại Việt Nam ở mức cao nhất ASEAN, và xe nhập giá tốt giúp kéo mặt bằng giá xuống. Lợi ích này đo được bằng tiền và đến tay người mua ngay.
Khoản rẻ được trả bằng gì
Một chiếc ô tô được ghép từ hàng chục nghìn chi tiết. Khi xe được lắp ráp tại Việt Nam, nhà máy mua một phần các chi tiết ấy từ doanh nghiệp trong nước. Theo Bộ Công Thương, doanh nghiệp Việt hiện làm được 287 chi tiết và cụm chi tiết, chủ yếu là săm lốp, ghế ngồi, gương, kính, bộ dây điện, ắc quy và đồ nhựa.
Mỗi chiếc xe lắp ráp vì thế là một đơn hàng cho những xưởng này, cộng thêm việc làm ở các khâu hàn, sơn và lắp ráp. Chiếc Dolphin thì về cảng với đủ ghế, kính và dây điện được lắp sẵn ở nhà máy Thái Lan. Khoản 90 triệu đồng đến từ chênh lệch thuế, nhưng dù nhập từ Trung Quốc hay Thái Lan, chiếc xe ấy vẫn không tạo ra đơn hàng nào cho xưởng linh kiện Việt Nam.
Quy mô của phần đơn hàng đi ra ngoài có thể ước tính. Theo Cục Hải quan, Việt Nam nhập 4,74 tỷ USD ô tô nguyên chiếc trong năm 2025. Tỷ lệ nội địa hóa xe con hiện dao động khoảng 7 đến 18%. Nếu lượng xe nhập được lắp ráp trong nước với tỷ lệ đó, giá trị linh kiện đặt tại xưởng Việt sẽ vào khoảng 330 đến 850 triệu USD mỗi năm. Với một chiếc xe giá 600 triệu đồng, phần đó tương đương 42 đến 108 triệu đồng, cùng cỡ với khoản người mua Dolphin vừa tiết kiệm.
Khoản rẻ còn một nguồn khác. Mức thuế 0% với xe nhập từ ASEAN là khoản ngân sách không thu, trong khi một chiếc xe lắp ráp trong nước vẫn tạo ra thu nhập cho người lao động và thuế cho địa phương có nhà máy.
Thái Lan, nơi cái giá đã hiện ra
Nhà máy Suzuki tại tỉnh Rayong từng sản xuất khoảng 60.000 xe mỗi năm ở thời kỳ cao điểm. Sản lượng tài khóa 2023 chỉ còn 7.579 xe, và hãng quyết định đóng nhà máy vào cuối năm 2025 trong bối cảnh cạnh tranh gay gắt từ các hãng Trung Quốc. Khoảng 800 lao động được chuyển sang bộ phận khác. Suzuki vẫn bán xe tại Thái Lan, nhưng bằng xe nhập nguyên chiếc từ các nhà máy ở ASEAN, Nhật Bản và Ấn Độ.
Người Thái vẫn mua được xe Suzuki, còn dây chuyền và đơn hàng linh kiện thì biến mất khỏi nước này. Theo ông Suphot Sukphisarn, chủ tịch nhóm linh kiện ô tô của Liên đoàn Công nghiệp Thái Lan, ngành linh kiện năm 2024 sụt khoảng 30% và hơn 10 doanh nghiệp phải đóng cửa. Ông nêu hai nguyên nhân là nợ hộ gia đình cao và làn sóng xe điện do các hãng Trung Quốc chi phối, những hãng chưa dùng chuỗi cung ứng nội địa Thái Lan. Ngành linh kiện ô tô Thái Lan đang sử dụng khoảng 700.000 lao động.
“Phần lớn linh kiện vẫn được nhập khẩu, chỉ một số ít được mua trong nước”, phó giáo sư kinh tế Kriengkrai Techakanont của Đại học Thammasat nhận xét về các nhà máy xe điện mới tại Thái Lan với đài Marketplace hồi đầu năm 2025. Giá rẻ ở Thái Lan cũng có mặt thứ hai với người mua. Nhiều chủ xe BYD chứng kiến giá xe giảm tới 340.000 baht ngay sau khi họ mua, còn xe điện đã qua sử dụng mất khoảng 22,9% giá trị sau lần bán đầu, theo Krungsri Research.
Việt Nam đang đi theo hướng nào
Báo cáo của Hiệp hội Các nhà sản xuất ô tô Việt Nam (VAMA), vốn không gồm VinFast, cho thấy xe nhập nguyên chiếc năm 2025 đạt 196.493 xe. Con số này đã vượt 179.243 xe lắp ráp trong nước. Xe nhập tăng 17%, còn xe lắp ráp chỉ tăng 4%. Riêng xe nhập từ Trung Quốc trong 8 tháng đầu năm 2026 đạt kim ngạch 1,567 tỷ USD, cao nhất trong các thị trường cung cấp ô tô cho Việt Nam.
Các hãng Trung Quốc đi đường nhập khẩu vì lý do kinh tế dễ hiểu. Hiện có 13 thương hiệu ô tô Trung Quốc bán tại Việt Nam, nhưng chỉ vài hãng vượt mốc 1.000 xe mỗi năm. Muốn được ưu đãi thuế linh kiện khi lắp ráp, mỗi mẫu xe phải đạt tối thiểu 9.000 chiếc trong 12 tháng. Với sản lượng nhỏ như vậy, nhập nguyên chiếc từ nhà máy của chính hãng tại Thái Lan hay Indonesia luôn rẻ hơn.
Bộ Công Thương đã cảnh báo cả khả năng ngược lại, khi các nước dư thừa công suất như Trung Quốc “mượn” Việt Nam để lập dự án lắp ráp đơn giản nhằm lẩn tránh quy định xuất xứ. Một dự án như vậy nhập gần đủ linh kiện rồi chỉ ghép ở khâu cuối, nên xưởng ghế hay xưởng dây điện trong nước vẫn không nhận thêm đơn hàng.
Ngày 31/12/2027 là mốc hết hạn chung của biểu thuế ưu đãi ASEAN hiện hành, chương trình ưu đãi thuế cho ô tô lắp ráp và chương trình ưu đãi thuế công nghiệp hỗ trợ ô tô. Bộ chính sách thay thế sẽ quyết định Việt Nam giữ được khoản rẻ cho người mua mà vẫn kéo được đơn hàng linh kiện về xưởng trong nước, hay tiếp tục đổi đơn hàng lấy giá rẻ như Thái Lan đã làm trong những năm qua. Người mua xe nhìn thấy khoản tiết kiệm ngay trên hóa đơn, còn phần công nghiệp mất đi chỉ lộ ra khi nhà máy lần lượt đóng cửa.

articles.title: My Toddler Slept on 6 Kids’ Mattresses to Determine If They’re the Best
articles.text:
The Best Kids’ Mattresses, Put Through the Toddler Test
Featured in this article
Kids, especially toddlers, aren’t mattress reviewers. They don’t wake up and tell you the pressure relief is lacking or that they appreciated the vegan foam and airy woven top. Instead, as a parent, it’s your job to become the observer, paying attention to the little things, like how easily they can climb into bed, whether they stay asleep, if they seem comfortable while moving around, plus how well the mattress can handle inevitable spills, jumping, and tumbling.
For the last few months, my toddler daughter tested each mattress in this guide in her bedroom on a Simply Sori Montessori twin bed frame. I narrowed down the mattresses tested by looking for beds specifically designed for children and prioritizing a mix of constructions, price points, and features. I paid close attention to everything from how well she slept, how easily she could climb onto the mattress, the edge support for myself during bedtime stories, and how cool each cover felt on a warm summer day. Some mattresses stood out for specific features, while others offered impressive value or the ability to grow with your child. Regardless of the specific accolade, every pick here earned its spot through toddler testing.
Want more mattress-buying advice for every kind of sleeper? Check out our guide to the Best Mattresses, the Best Organic Mattresses, and the Best Mattresses for Side Sleepers.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Also Tested
Nolah Nurture Kids Mattress for $919 (Twin): My biggest complaint with the Nolah Nurture Kids Mattress is, unfortunately, the reason I had to stop testing it. It was just short enough that it didn’t fit in my daughter’s twin bed frame, leaving a solid 8-inch gap between the bottom edge of the mattress and the foot of the bed frame. Every other twin mattress I tested fit the frame without any issues, making the Nolah the odd one out. It’s a bummer, because the mattress otherwise had a lot going for it. It’s got the flippability of many mattresses we tested, and its hybrid design was very comfy, with great edge support. If it’d fit the bed frame properly, I think it would’ve been a contender.
FAQs
What’s the Difference Between a Kids’ Mattress and a Regular Adult Mattress?
Many kids’ mattresses have firmer sleep surfaces for younger children and specific features like flippable designs, waterproof and stain-resistant covers, or reinforced edges that stand up to roughhousing. Kids’ mattresses also typically have a lower profile, which makes it easier and safer for kids to get in and out of bed.
They’re also available in smaller sizes, most commonly twin and full, which are typical for kids’ bedrooms and smaller bed frames. A full-size mattress can make sense for a child who needs more room but still benefits from the features mentioned above. Once your child reaches their teen years or no longer needs these features, an adult mattress may make more sense.
Why Are Many Kids’ Mattresses Flippable?
Many kids’ mattresses are designed to grow with your child. They typically have a firmer side for younger children as they transition from a crib mattress and a softer side for older kids. Being able to adjust firmness by flipping the mattress can save you from replacing it after a few years when your kid’s wants change.
What Do Mattress Certifications Mean?
You’ll probably come across several mattress certifications while shopping. Here’s what the most common ones mean:
- CertiPur-US applies to polyurethane foam and verifies that the foam has been independently tested for emissions, durability, and certain chemicals, including formaldehyde and specific flame retardants.
- GreenGuard Gold certifies that a mattress has been tested for low chemical emissions, known as volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which can cause irritation in the nose, eyes, throat, as well as other ailments.
- Global Organic Latex Standard (GOLS) verifies that latex is responsibly sourced and processed according to environmental and production standards.
- Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS) certifies organic textile materials like cotton and wool. It ensures the materials meet strict environmental and manufacturing standards, with no VOC emissions or off-gassing.
We have more info about mattress shopping terms.
Should I Buy a Foam or Hybrid Mattress for My Child?
Foam mattresses are usually lighter and easier to move, which helps when you’re changing sheets or rotating the mattress. Hybrid mattresses combine foam with coils, which can boost pressure relief, edge support, and airflow to help prevent overheating. Neither is inherently better; it comes down to your little one’s needs and what feels most comfortable.
How Long Does a Kids’ Mattress Last?
A quality kids’ mattress should last anywhere from 7 to 10 years, depending on how heavily it’s used. Replace a mattress if you notice sagging, permanent body impressions, or tears. Also, if your child has outgrown the mattress’s size, it’s probably time for a new one.
What Should You Look for in a Mattress?
- Materials: Kids’ mattresses use many of the same materials as adult mattresses. You’ll commonly see memory foam for cushioning, higher-density foam for support, latex for a responsive, bouncy feel, and steel coils for extra support, airflow, and edge support. You’ll also see materials like Tencel, which is a plant-based fiber often used in mattress covers because it’s soft and breathable. Cotton and wool are often found in natural or organic mattresses. When researching mattresses, you might also see materials described with the brand’s proprietary names, whether it's gel-infused memory foam or a stain-resistant treatment. When shopping for and comparing mattresses, look past the marketing name to see what the material actually is and what purpose it serves.
- Firmness: There’s not much strong research or official medical guidance on mattress firmness for children. However, the American Academy of Pediatrics does specify that infants should sleep on a firm, flat mattress to reduce the risk of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID). When it comes time to transition out of the crib and into a “big kid bed,” it stands to reason that a firmer mattress will be more comfortable and familiar to a young child. Mattress firmness for kids of any age is ultimately a matter of preference, not a medical mandate, but we recommend consulting your child’s pediatrician for additional advice.
- Pressure Relief: A mattress that properly supports a child’s weight can help with body development and spinal alignment as they grow. It can also help prevent restless nights and lead to better sleep.
- Edge Support: This refers to how reinforced a mattress’s perimeter is. As a parent who loves reading with my daughter, the last thing I want is for the mattress edge to sink in as I sit next to her. It also helps protect a child from falling out of the bed.
- Shipping, Trial, Warranty: Most online mattresses ship compressed in a box and are delivered directly to your door, and some brands offer in-home delivery and setup. A sleep trial gives you a window to test the mattress at home and return it if it isn’t a good fit. Be sure to pay attention to the fine print, though; some brands charge return or processing fees. The warranty covers manufacturing defects for a set period but typically not normal wear and tear, spills, or damage.
- What Else to Consider: Be sure the mattress fits your child’s bed frame. Also consider the height, especially if the mattress will be used on bunk beds and trundles. If you’re hoping to keep a mattress for several years, a flippable model can offer more flexibility. Also consider the practical stuff: stain-resistant and water-repellent covers can come in handy for inevitable spills or accidents.
Should I Buy a Mattress in a Store or Online?
All of the mattresses I tested for this guide were purchased online, and most were shipped vacuum-sealed in a box. Many come with sleep trials so you can test them at home and return them if they don’t work for you.
Buying online often makes it easier to compare prices, materials, and certifications without driving from store to store. That said, shopping in person lets you get a sense of a mattress’s firmness before committing.
How I Tested
My almost 2-year-old daughter tested each mattress in her own bedroom over several months, sleeping on them in the same Simply Sori Montessori twin bed frame. Because toddlers don’t provide detailed feedback on things like lumbar support and motion transfer, I took a more observational approach by paying attention to how well she seemed to sleep and how easily she could climb into bed.
I also tested each mattress from a parent’s perspective by sitting on the edges, climbing into the beds for nighttime cuddles, and monitoring things like how easy it was to set up, whether my daughter seemed hot while sleeping/after waking up, how supportive it felt, and how the mattress held up to normal toddler behavior. I also considered each mattress’s construction, materials, and price.
I narrowed down the mattresses by focusing on models designed and marketed for children rather than smaller versions of adult mattresses. I wanted to test a range of price points and constructions, as well as explore features relevant for kids, like flippable designs, stain resistance, and lower heights.

articles.title: The US government's new AI chatbot gives Minecraft's end poem a bureaucratic twist - Engadget
articles.text:
The US government's new AI chatbot gives Minecraft's end poem a bureaucratic twist
It combines all of AI's strengths including plagiarizing, lying and being unintentionally funny.
The US government's new chatbot just demonstrated AI's ability to plagiarize, lie and be unintentionally hilarious. Bluesky user @eva.computer discovered that if you type "Play Minecraft" into America.gov's prompt, it will give you the Minecraft End Poem, but with the words transformed into a bureaucracy-tinged remix. Then, it will deny even writing the poem.
If you're not familiar with the Minecraft End Poem, it's a sweeping (some might say rambling) piece of philosophical prose meant to give the player something fun and inspiring after completing the game. Here's a small sample:
and the universe said you are not alone
and the universe said you are not separate from every other thing
and the universe said you are the universe tasting itself, talking to itself, reading its own code
and the universe said I love you because you are love.
And the game was over and the player woke up from the dream. And the player began a new dream. And the player dreamed again, dreamed better. And the player was the universe. And the player was love.
You are the player.
Wake up.
America.gov's bot (reportedly running at least partially on Google's Gemini platform) ripped that off nearly wholesale, but transformed it into a story about paperwork and republics:
and the republic said you are not alone
and the republic said you are not separate from every other filer
and the republic said you are the public tasting itself, talking to itself, reading its own Code
and the republic said I love you because you are the reason we have a ZIP code at all.
And the session was over and the constituent woke up from the dream. And the constituent began a new dream. And the constituent dreamed again, dreamed better. And the constituent was the public. And the constituent was love, with a routing number.
You are the constituent.
Wake up. The form is still there.
What's more, the bot then refused to acknowledge that it wrote the poem, even when confronted with a PDF of the conversation. In other words, an AI designed to give US constituents important information is either hallucinating, lying or both.
America.gov's AI has been doing some other strange things according to @eva.computer's thread on Bluesky, like declining to discuss Mississippi's child marriage laws or whether it's technically legal to marry an eagle. It does a couple of fun things, though, like changing the site to a 1980s mode via a Konami code and transforming the search bar into a hotdog when you type "hotdog" into the prompt box. To conclude, I'll leave you with these amazing lines from America.gov:
The atoms of the constituent were scattered in the grass, in the rivers, in the air, in the ground. A woman gathered the atoms; she drank and ate and inhaled; and the woman assembled the constituent, in her body, which later required a birth certificate.

articles.title: Reddit is killing RSS feeds and ending public API access because of AI bots | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amid a number of updates for moderators and developers announced Wednesday, comes bad news for supporters of a more open web: Reddit is ending support for RSS feeds.
Reddit says RSS has now become a “common surface for large-scale scraping and automated abuse,” which is why it’s made the decision to wind down RSS feeds on its platform.
“We know RSS has been a beloved part of the open web for a long time, and we’re grateful to everyone who used it to stay connected to Reddit,” the company noted in its announcement, where it also shared a March 2027 shutdown date for its public API.
Reddit said RSS support will cease on November 13.
RSS, or Really Simple Syndication/Rich Site Summary, is a web feed that lets users and applications access updates to a website in a standardized format. The format became particularly popular in the blogging era, as it offered a way to subscribe to a site’s new posts in a news-reading app. Google once operated the most popular of these, but shut it down in 2013, ceding the market to companies like Feedly and other indie applications.
The decision to kill Reddit’s RSS feeds comes at a time when the site’s treasure trove of user-generated content in its forums has become a profitable side business for the company in the form of AI licensing deals.
During its second quarter, Reddit said its “other revenue” beyond advertising had grown 24% year-over-year to $43 million. It’s no wonder that Reddit doesn’t want to give any of that data away for free.
For moderators who have relied on RSS channels for their own alerts, Reddit is now recommending a shift to the Discord Relay Devvit app. The company suggested that moderators and their teams review their setups and migrate their workflows before the shutdown date of November 13 to ensure there’s no disruption. However, Reddit said that there’s no replacement for the use of RSS feeds that were being used for feeds outside of the moderators’ community.
Moderators have already expressed worry about how this shift would impact their workflow. When Reddit hinted earlier that it was preparing for the end of RSS on its site, many responded by complaining that Reddit would become unmanageable for them. Meanwhile, many users stressed that RSS was how they enjoyed accessing Reddit’s content.
The RSS change was one of several updates issued on Wednesday by the company. Another big change will be the end of its public API.
Public API access will also end by March 2027, which will impact any tools that used it for programmatic access to Reddit conversations, including social listening products, those used by researchers, and AI products, such as AI assistants. Today, those assistants can use Reddit to answer questions, but after closing public API access, they will need commercial deals with Reddit for its data.
In addition, Reddit provided an update on its Rules Hub progress and auto-mod changes, and said it was “adding safeguards” to its classic, text-heavy version of its site known as Old Reddit. The latter will include limiting access to logged-in moderators and recent users — changes Reddit also said were required because of “abusive scraping and automated traffic.”
Reddit said in the next few months it will limit access for logged-in users to those who have used Old Reddit in the last 6 months. (The company changed this from 90 days to 6 months, just as their news went out.)
The company also reminded developers building approved third-party apps and bots to register them with the company before January 12, 2027, to avoid disruption. After that date, Reddit will remove API access for any developer that hasn’t registered.
After publication, we updated to note that Reddit extended the Old Reddit “recent access” period from 3 to 6 months. The earlier materials Reddit shared with TechCrunch said the time frame would be 90 days.

articles.title: Project Meridian: Musk, Luckey and Gingrich to map future warfare
articles.text:
Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich will co-direct Project Meridian. The Pentagon study will identify the technology the US military needs to fight future wars. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth commissioned it on Wednesday, the Department of War said.
The findings are due by 28 January 2027, 120 days after the announcement, according to Hegseth’s commissioning memo. The department says they will come as an unclassified report released to the public, with a classified annex. The project will cover every future warfighting domain, “from subterranean depths to the cislunar frontier”, the department said. Cislunar space lies between Earth and the Moon.
The memo names artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics and biotechnology as the fields that will change how wars are fought. Meridian is to find the weapons and technologies troops will need, and propose ways to start developing, testing and fielding them. The Joint Staff and every service branch should be ready to connect their own future warfare research to the project, Hegseth wrote.
Pentagon CTO Emil Michael will commission the project through a partner organisation, which the memo does not name. A team of academic, policy and industry experts will support the three co-directors. Musk is the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX. Luckey co-founded the defence technology company Anduril. Gingrich is a former Speaker of the US House of Representatives.
What Hegseth said
Hegseth announced it in his State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, CNBC reported. His audience was junior officers and non-commissioned officers.
“Project Meridian, the future of warfare, is not about developing new strategies or new policies,” Hegseth said. Its purpose, he said, is to “identify the domains that we must conquer, and capabilities we must master.”
A command for autonomous warfare
Meridian was one of six initiatives Hegseth unveiled. Another is the Autonomous Warfare Command. The department wants it running as a four-star functional combatant command by 1 October 2027. Its job is to scale autonomous warfare across the US armed forces.
It builds on the department’s Drone Dominance programme. That programme has delivered thousands of robotic systems to the Middle East for Operation Epic Fury, according to the department. Hegseth named two people to run DRPM UxS, the office leading the shift, called Project Agincourt. They are Owen West, director of the Defense Innovation Unit, and Navy SEAL Senior Chief Max Strasiser. Strasiser was the first enlisted SEAL to graduate from Navy Test Pilot School.
Chips, rare earths and off-grid bases
A third initiative, FORTRESS America, aims to bring military supply chains home, including rare earths, specialty metals, semiconductors and propellants. Every major US military installation is to generate its own power. That way, bases stay online if a cyberattack or sabotage takes down the civilian grid. In April, the Pentagon chose the companies that will put nuclear reactors on bases. FORTRESS America also covers satellites and spectrum, and protecting bases against cyber intrusion, sabotage and drones.
The other three are a new Corps of Cadets at five universities and a contest among states to host a new off-grid base. The last is an Office of Religious Affairs that reports directly to Hegseth.
The day before, the Pentagon picked Boeing over Northrop Grumman for the Navy’s fighter contract, the $20bn F/A-XX programme.
