articles.title: This blog could help you poop better
articles.text:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.
This blog could help you poop better
Fibermaxxing might help boost an underconsumed nutrient, but you should also be wary of ‘maxxing’ trends.
This blog could help you poop better
Fibermaxxing might help boost an underconsumed nutrient, but you should also be wary of ‘maxxing’ trends.
“I will explode your butthole with this poopmaxxer pesto,” a calm Gen Z voice announced from my phone’s speakers. “And don’t worry, it doesn’t taste like poop, unless that’s what you’re into … I don’t know if Italians will approve of this, but it’s for my … a-butt-a-hole-a!”
What followed in that video was actually a pretty good recipe. Two cups of blanched peas mixed into a fairly standard pesto recipe for a yield of 18 grams of fiber. Never mind my spouse’s flabbergasted face as the video played over and over while I blanched and blended in the kitchen.
Not all TikTok fibermaxxers are as disturbingly whimsical as @hallysicle, a self-described “chaotic wellness” creator responsible for the poopmaxxer pesto; the cognitive dissonance of her deadpan scatological narration, cottagecore kawaii aesthetic, and actually good recipes is very much her own creation. That said, many of TikTok’s fiberheads are gleefully unhinged when preaching the benefits of the criminally underappreciated and underconsumed macronutrient.
There’s Liam, a friendly nutritional fad debunker who’s also gained fame as “the Bean Guy” for his love of beans and fiber. He is regularly summoned in the comments of any bean recipe. (Once showing up as an actual ghostly beanfather.) On the other side of the spectrum, there’s Fiber Daddy — a dry influencer who says you’re being “a total dumdum” for throwing away your broccoli stems. He claims to poop four times daily and sells a supplement called Liquid Salad. But perhaps more surprising are the fiber-obsessed healthcare providers also jumping in on the trend.
Considering that roughly 95 percent of Americans fall short of the daily recommended amount of fiber, you’d think fibermaxxing is unequivocally a good thing. But as with anything on the internet, “maxxing” doesn’t always tell the whole story.
Why is the internet suddenly obsessed with fiber and pooping? There’s no single reason, but rather a few larger-scale health trends converging with the influencer content economy.
Take GLP-1 usage. The so-called Ozempic economy is one big reason why you’re seeing a huge push for fresh foods and proteinwashing at the grocery store. Because GLP-1s can suppress appetite, people on these medications have to prioritize protein and fiber in their diets to prevent muscle loss and alleviate gastrointestinal side effects. (One example: those Grüns gummy bears appealing to GLP-1 users in their marketing.) This affects an increasingly large portion of the population. A recent Gallup survey has found that in the US, GLP-1 usage has skyrocketed to 11 percent in 2026 from 3 percent just two years ago.
There’s also been a rising number of videos featuring young people in their 20s and 30s sharing their stories of battling colon cancer. These videos are often bolstered by social media-savvy gastroenterologists and dietitians who are also trying to raise awareness of this trend and early-onset symptoms. There are likely several reasons why colorectal cancer is on the rise, but one common refrain: Partaking in a fiber-rich diet can help reduce risk compared to the typical American diet.
The scary thing is that this isn’t baseless fearmongering or a viral trend taking science out of context. A recent study has found that mortality from colorectal cancer in people under 50 has been increasing by 1.1 percent per year since 2005, making it the leading cause of cancer-related death in this cohort. Today, the American Cancer Society estimates that 45 percent of new diagnoses come from people under 65 years old, a significant increase from 27 percent in 1995.
So all things considered, yes — fiber (and therefore, pooping) is on a lot of people’s minds. That, in turn, makes it ripe for contentmaxxing online.
In some respects, this could be a good thing. While RFK Jr.’s MAHA movement has zeroed in on protein — a nutrient that the vast majority of Americans are not deficient in — fiber is an important and consequential macronutrient that virtually everyone gets too little of. Put plainly, dietary fiber is a type of complex carbohydrate that the body can’t digest and primarily comes from plant foods. It also comes in two types: soluble and insoluble. The former dissolves in water, forming a gel-like substance in your gut that helps lower cholesterol and blood glucose levels. The latter helps add bulk to your poops, making them easier to pass and helps prevent constipation.
On top of these benefits, a high-fiber diet is associated with greater satiety — good for weight management — and overall bowel health by helping prevent hemorrhoids, feeding the beneficial bacteria in your gut microbiome, and, again, reducing overall colorectal cancer risk.
But as with any health trend, more is not always better. Not all fiber is created equal.
To be fair, the majority of fibermaxxers online tend to focus on fiber-rich diets featuring whole foods. Inspiration for palatable ways to sneak in veggies, oats, beans, or leafy greens during busy weeks, sometimes in quirky ways. That kind of fibermaxxing content is relatively harmless. You just might hear a lot about poop and see numerous poop emojis.
But social media often erases nuance to sell you something. And it’s only a matter of time before companies hawking fiber supplements hop on the bandwagon.
Three supplements I’ve previously covered in Optimizer are already doing this. There’s AG1, which has a whole fiber page to promote its Essentials Gummies product. (It’s more famous greens powder only has 2g of fiber, after all.) Huel, a meal replacement drink, sells a fiber boost bundle. And then there’s the aforementioned Grüns, which prominently features its 6g of fiber per pack in its marketing. Considering how the commercial food industry is stuffing protein into every product, it wouldn’t take much for fibermaxxed versions of ultra-processed foods to start hitting shelves — if they haven’t already.
As part of a diverse diet, fiber supplements aren’t the worst thing. The problem is you need both soluble and insoluble fiber in your diet to get all the benefits. Supplements tend to overindex on inulin, psyllium husk, or tapioca fiber — all of which are soluble and, in excess, can cause a lot of gas. (Turns out, a soluble source is generally easier to incorporate into various forms.) Fiber supplements have their time and place! But it’s also in the name. They’re meant to supplement in a pinch, not be the convenient way to get fiber while avoiding plants in your diet.
Speaking of gas, some fibermaxxers are actually advocating for fartmaxxing with absurd goals like 60 to 100g of fiber per day. Technically, there is no official upper limit to fiber. The unofficial limit is what your digestive system can handle. Just as a diet full of diverse fiber sources can alleviate gas and bloating, going ham on fiber intake too quickly can cause gastrointestinal distress. (Beans have a reputation for a reason.) The daily recommended amount of fiber is roughly 14 grams per 1,000 calories — or 25 to 38g per day depending on age and caloric needs. Health experts and the literature largely agree that’s what most people should aspire to, slowly, gradually, and with lots of water to mitigate negative side effects until the digestive system adjusts.
Lastly, not everyone can boost their fiber intake willy-nilly. Those with Crohn’s disease, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, or bowel obstructions need to consult their doctors. The same goes for people on certain thyroid, cardiovascular, diabetes, and depression medications. Fiber supplements, for example, can interfere with absorption and make a drug less effective, so meal timing becomes more important.
Of all the “maxxing” trends, fibermaxxing has been one of the less problematic. (So far.) Most dietitians and gastroenterologists would likely rejoice if more people strolled into their appointments asking for help in boosting fiber intake. But in the wellness wild west, things can get stupid real fast. Part of why maxxing hits so hard with health trends is that it taps into fearmongering — often about genuine concerns based on a modicum of science — with an easy black-and-white solution. Social media creators, including well-intentioned ones, hop onto sound bites to gain views, and then affiliate partnership deals to keep the lights on. Nuance is tragically less viral.
The truth is, doctors have been telling us all to prioritize fiber for decades. Eat the rainbow. Prioritize whole foods. Make sure to eat a serving of veggies with each meal. Whole grains over refined grains! All of these could be considered the OG fibermaxxing commandments. They’ll also still be true once the fibermaxxing moment has given way to the next eye-searing, brain-breaking health fad.

articles.title: Google launches Fitbit Air in India, though its high price might deter the masses | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google on Wednesday launched the screen-less Fitbit Air fitness tracker in India, but is pricing it at ₹13,999 (roughly $146), ostensibly positioning it as a premium device. Comparatively, the device costs $99 in the U.S.
Unveiled in May, the Fitbit Air features health and fitness tracking, like 24/7 heart rate monitoring, heart rhythm monitoring with A-fib (atrial fibrillation) alerts, blood oxygen level, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep stages, and duration.
The device’s screen-less form is a bid to tap into the growing popularity of screen-less devices as people shy away from screens, opting for distraction-free health gadgets like Whoop’s fitness bands and Oura’s rings — though the new Fitbit is more pocket-friendly.
The health tracking space now has screen-less devices from Garmin, Fitbit founders’ new company, Luffu Link, as well as from Indian startups like Noise and Urban, which have been trying to undercut their Western rivals on price.
Research firm IDC noted in its global wearables report that despite a declining number of wristband shipments, screen-less trackers are carving out a niche. India currently accounts for only 5% of the screenless wearable market, per Counterpoint Research, and a wearable priced like a premium device might not make a dent in overall numbers, despite having a big name like Fitbit or Google behind it.
The Fitbit Air is available for purchase on the Google Store and retail partners, including Flipkart, Croma, Reliance Digital, and Vijay Sales, from October 2. Google is also offering a free, three-month Google Health premium membership with the new band.

articles.title: Từ ký ức tuổi thơ đến tủ đồ hiện đại: Vì sao những món đồ gợi nhớ “Việt Nam ngày xưa” đang được yêu thích trở lại?
articles.text:
Những hình ảnh từng xuất hiện trên áo lưu niệm, biển hiệu, tranh ảnh hay trong ký ức tuổi thơ nay được nhiều thương hiệu thời trang khai thác theo cách mới: bớt trực diện, nhiều tính sáng tạo hơn và quan trọng nhất là gần với trải nghiệm cá nhân.
Có một thời, những chiếc áo phông in dòng chữ “I Love Vietnam”, hình Vịnh Hạ Long, chợ Bến Thành hay những địa danh nổi tiếng thường được xem như món đồ lưu niệm dành cho khách du lịch. Với nhiều người trẻ Việt, chúng thậm chí từng gắn với cảm giác “quê”, thiếu cá tính và không đủ thời trang để mặc hàng ngày.
Nhưng cách nhìn ấy đang thay đổi. Những hình ảnh từng xuất hiện trên áo lưu niệm, biển hiệu, tranh ảnh hay trong ký ức tuổi thơ nay được nhiều thương hiệu thời trang khai thác theo cách mới nhiều tính sáng tạo hơn và quan trọng nhất là gần với trải nghiệm cá nhân.
Khi một món đồ gợi nhớ đến hàng quà tuổi thơ, món ăn vỉa hè hay con phố quen thuộc, nó không chỉ mang giá trị thẩm mỹ. Nó còn đánh thức cảm giác về một thời điểm, một nơi chốn và những điều tưởng như đã rất quen thuộc.
Khi những điều từng bị xem là “quê” trở thành chất liệu thời trang
Sự trở lại của những hình ảnh “rất Việt” không đơn thuần là việc đưa các biểu tượng cũ lên những chiếc áo mới. Điểm khác biệt nằm ở cách chúng được kể lại.
Thay vì in nguyên một địa danh với dòng chữ lớn, các thương hiệu có thể chọn một chi tiết nhỏ của đời sống để phát triển thành graphic. Thay vì tái hiện nguyên xi hình ảnh truyền thống, họ biến đổi màu sắc, bố cục, chất liệu hoặc cách minh họa để phù hợp với thẩm mỹ hiện tại. Điều này tạo ra một nghịch lý thú vị: càng quen thuộc, những hình ảnh ấy đôi khi càng dễ tạo cảm giác mới mẻ khi được đặt trong một bối cảnh khác.
Một gánh hàng rong, chiếc xe đạp, khu chợ, món ăn đường phố hay một câu nói quen thuộc vốn chẳng có gì đặc biệt khi xuất hiện trong đời sống. Nhưng khi trở thành hình in trên áo, poster hay phụ kiện, chúng lại có thể khiến người mặc nhớ đến một con phố từng đi qua, một món ăn tuổi thơ hoặc những ngày còn nhỏ đi chơi cùng gia đình.
Hoài niệm đang trở thành một phần của phong cách cá nhân
Một lý do khiến những chất liệu này dễ kết nối với người trẻ nằm ở sức mạnh của nostalgia - cảm giác hoài niệm về những trải nghiệm trong quá khứ.
Trong thời trang, nostalgia không nhất thiết đồng nghĩa với việc mặc lại nguyên một phong cách cũ. Quan trọng hơn là lấy một chi tiết từng quen thuộc và đặt nó vào ngữ cảnh mới. Đó có thể là một graphic mang hơi hướng retro, kiểu chữ gợi nhớ những tấm biển cũ, hình ảnh món ăn quen thuộc hay một biểu tượng văn hóa được tối giản hóa. Người mặc vẫn đang sử dụng một món đồ rất hiện đại, nhưng câu chuyện phía sau lại thuộc về một phần ký ức.
Vì vậy, một chiếc áo gợi nhớ “Việt Nam ngày xưa” có thể hấp dẫn không phải vì nó cũ, mà vì nó tạo ra cảm giác riêng. Người mặc không đơn thuần lựa chọn một thiết kế đẹp; họ cũng đang lựa chọn một hình ảnh có khả năng kể điều gì đó về bản thân.
Khi ký ức Việt được đưa vào tủ đồ theo một cách mới
Có những hình ảnh không cần giải thích vẫn đủ khiến người Việt nhận ra mình đang nhìn thấy một phần ký ức quen thuộc. Đó có thể là một gánh hàng rong, món ăn trên vỉa hè, khu chợ đông người hay một góc phố từng đi qua hàng trăm lần. Với CANIFA S, những chất liệu như vậy trở thành nguồn cảm hứng để kể lại Việt Nam bằng thời trang dành cho đời sống hiện đại.
Ở Việt Nam Yêu Đời, thương hiệu đưa những lát cắt bình dị của cuộc sống vào thiết kế, từ hàng rong, món ăn đến những khoảnh khắc gia đình. Trạm Yêu Nước lại khai thác cảm xúc tự hào qua màu sắc và tinh thần gắn kết, trong khi Hội Ngọ tìm đến hình tượng ngựa để tạo nên câu chuyện về năng lượng, chuyển động và khát vọng.
Cách tiếp cận này khiến những hình ảnh vốn quen thuộc có thêm một đời sống mới. Thay vì chỉ xuất hiện trong ký ức hoặc trên những món đồ lưu niệm sau chuyến du lịch, chúng có thể trở thành một phần của phong cách cá nhân một cách khá tự nhiên để người mặc mang theo câu chuyện về nơi mình thuộc về.
Từ đồ lưu niệm đến món đồ có thể mặc mỗi ngày
Sự thay đổi này cũng cho thấy ranh giới giữa “đồ lưu niệm” và “thời trang” đang trở nên linh hoạt hơn. Trước đây, một chiếc áo in hình địa danh thường có mục đích khá rõ: mua về để nhớ một chuyến đi. Ngày nay, cùng một tinh thần ấy có thể được xử lý thành một thiết kế đủ phù hợp để mặc trong nhiều hoàn cảnh khác nhau.
Đó là lúc ký ức trở thành một phần của thiết kế thay vì toàn bộ thiết kế. Người mặc không cần phải “mặc một món đồ Việt Nam” theo nghĩa trực diện. Họ chỉ cần bắt gặp một hình ảnh khiến mình thấy thân thuộc. Có lẽ đây cũng là lý do những câu chuyện về “Việt Nam ngày xưa” có thể tìm được chỗ đứng trong tủ đồ hiện đại. Bởi sau cùng, điều khiến một thiết kế trở nên đáng nhớ đôi khi không nằm ở việc nó mới đến đâu, mà ở việc nó khiến người mặc nhớ đến điều gì.

articles.title: Boeing beats Northrop to build the US Navy's $20bn F/A-XX fighter
articles.text:
Boeing will build the US Navy’s next carrier-based fighter, the F/A-XX, after beating Northrop Grumman for the contract. The Pentagon announced the award on Tuesday.
The development contract is worth 0bn to produce test aircraft, Reuters reported. CNBC and Axios put it at more than 0bn. The programme could grow to hundreds of billions of dollars over its lifetime, according to Reuters.
“It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform,” Steve Parker, chief executive of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said in a statement.
What the jet replaces
The F/A-XX will replace the F/A-18 Super Hornet, which Boeing also builds. The Super Hornet has flown from carriers since the 1990s. It will fly alongside the Lockheed Martin F-35C. Its design details remain classified, Boeing said.
The jet should be stealthy, fly farther and work with uncrewed aircraft, Reuters reported. The first production jets are due in the 2030s.
Michael Duffey, the Pentagon’s chief weapons buyer, called it “a crucial, non-negotiable investment” in US security.
Boeing’s second sixth-generation win
The award is Boeing’s second sixth-generation fighter in two years. The Air Force picked it for the F-47 in 2025.
Some Pentagon officials had sought to delay the Navy jet by up to three years, citing engineering and supply-chain capacity, Reuters reported. Congress pushed back and funded the programme. The Navy knocked Lockheed out of the competition in March 2025.
Boeing shares rose 2.25% in extended trading on Tuesday, and Northrop fell 3.5%, according to Reuters. Boeing is building what it calls the largest secure manufacturing facility in the US, in St. Louis.
The Pentagon has also been handing out large contracts for its Golden Dome missile shield, including .16bn to SpaceX. The Space Force tailored some of that work to suit SpaceX, Bloomberg reported. Startups are building AI-piloted fighter jets too.

articles.title: Asus won’t say how it escaped the US router ban
articles.text:
This spring, the United States banned all future foreign-made consumer routers — effectively all future routers — unless their makers could 1) convince the US government that they weren’t a national security threat, and 2) submit “a detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.”
Asus won’t say how it escaped the US router ban
Asus is not publicly committing to US manufacturing.
As of September 9th, Asus now has an exemption from the ban, just in time to bring its first early Wi-Fi 8 routers here. But Asus has not publicly announced any plan to bring manufacturing to the US. It would not even confirm to The Verge whether it had submitted a US manufacturing plan.
Initially, Asus spokesperson JJ Guerrero forwarded the following statement to The Verge: “ASUS has submitted the required plan to the FCC and is working with trusted manufacturing partners to support our future networking product portfolio in the U.S.”
But when we repeatedly asked Asus to clarify whether that meant it had submitted a plan to manufacture equipment in the United States — as opposed to equipment that’s just for the United States — the company did not answer. We’ve been waiting over 12 days without clarification.
The US router ban is not about security, despite the government’s claims. The FCC doesn’t ask companies a single question about security to get an exemption from the ban; it’s more about where routers are made. Nor is the FCC carefully testing which products are safe and which might have security holes — it has granted Asus a blanket exemption on all future routers through March 2028.
Few consumer products are made in the United States these days for all kinds of economic reasons. Even a copy of the board game Monopoly is now difficult to manufacture domestically. It wouldn’t be surprising if Asus wants to avoid building factories here.
But if the US router ban is not about US manufacturing, and it’s not about security, what is it actually about? Why did the Trump administration suddenly give Asus a blanket exemption, and why did it give Netgear a similar blanket exemption back in April?
The FCC did not respond to a request for comment then, and it has not responded to our fact-check request for this story. Perhaps it’s simply satisfied that these companies aren’t making them in China; both Asus and Netgear claim they’re manufacturing in countries that are considered US allies, and Netgear additionally says that “we no longer procure internet-connected components from manufacturers in China, or entities owned or controlled by China.”
Publicly, both Asus and Netgear are using the US government’s exemptions as marketing tools. In April, Netgear even emailed existing customers to share the news that Netgear is a “trusted consumer router company” now. Asus now claims it passed a “rigorous cybersecurity review” and is now certified as a “Trusted Networking Equipment Brand” and listed as a “Trusted Consumer Router Vendor,” as if those were official terms.
But search results for “Trusted Networking Equipment Brand” and “Trusted Consumer Router Vendor” only point back to Asus’s own claims — not the federal government.

articles.title: Instagram rolls out an AI video assistant for creators | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Instagram announced on Wednesday that it’s bringing an AI video assistant tool to Edits, its CapCut competitor.
This conversational AI chatbot is intended to provide personalized feedback to creators, rather than generic advice.
“The assistant knows your account’s Instagram metrics, things like follows, views, video retention, likes, shares and combines them with your comments, what’s trending on Instagram and what your audience is into,” Brett Westervelt, who leads the Edits app, said. “It can spot patterns in your performance over time and surface actionable insights that are hard to see from the metrics alone.”
Westervelt added that Edits worked closely with a group of creators in developing the tool.
“One thing we heard consistently: creators want a tool that handles the analysis, not one that does the creative work for them,” he wrote. “Edits assistant does the digging for you. The creative calls are still yours.”
Meta first previewed the Edits AI assistant in June at an invite-only creator event, where it also said it was working on an Edits desktop app. It’s not the only company working on tools like this, though. YouTube announced last week that it is also working on a conversational video editing tool, which should be available early next year.
From what we can tell so far, it looks like Meta is taking a more analytics-driven approach with its AI assistant than YouTube, which suggested creators would use its AI to help with the actual editing process.
Creators will have a limit to how much they can use the AI tool, but they can unlock more usage with a Meta One subscription.

articles.title: Inside India newsletter: Foreign insurers get the red-carpet treatment — and policy uncertainty
articles.text:
Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.
Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.
India's insurance sector has held a lot of promise for global companies, given low penetration rates and consequent reforms that have liberalized the industry. But recently proposed rules reintroducing commission caps could pour cold water on insurers' plans.
Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.
The big story
Global insurers eager for a bigger slice of the world's 10th-largest insurance market, after it allowed for 100% foreign ownership in the sector last December, are in for a rude surprise as the country's regulator plans to reverse one of its key reforms.
Last week, India's insurance regulator proposed the reintroduction of product-level commission caps, reversing its move in 2023 that allowed insurers flexibility over their commission structures.
While India's insurance market remains a long-term opportunity, experts warned that operational complexities ushered in by the frequent shifts in policy will make foreign investors pause their plans. If the proposals are agreed upon, insurers will have to comply by year ending March 2029.
The market was primed for cross-border deal activity after the foreign direct investment limit was raised to 100%, Debashish Banerjee, partner and insurance sector leader at Deloitte India, told CNBC.
But deals will be paused as managements and boards of foreign insurers will need to deliberate on the recent changes, he said, adding that more importantly, discussions will hinge on "what if six months down the road there will be another policy change?"
On Sept. 23, the regulator proposed new rules that seek to reinstate commission caps, tighten expense management limits and restructure remunerations to reward policy renewals instead of upfront sales volume.
State-owned firms such as the Life Insurance Corporation, SBI Life and New India Assurance are already operating within the proposed caps, as per local media reports. Other insurance companies, however, will need to cut total management expenses sharply, according to Indian credit rating agency Care Edge.
The proposals require private life insurers to cut total management expenses from 20% to 15% of gross direct premium income within two years and to 12.5% within five years, and general insurers to reduce it from 30% to 20% over five years, according to Care Ratings said.
"20 of 22 life insurers and 28 of 31 general insurers are above the proposed FY29 expense ceiling," the agency said.
Insurers take a hit
Currently, the commission structures are very front-ended, with almost 35%-40% being paid out up-front to agents and the middlemen, which led to a lot of mis-selling of insurance products, Ramkumar Subramanian, partner for insurance at Grant Thornton Bharat, told CNBC.
The regulator wants to arrest this trend through the proposed changes, he said.
The market, however, was not thrilled with the announcement. A day after the new rules were proposed, India's largest online platform for insurance policies PB Fintech saw shares crash 36%, HDFC Life fell more than 6% and ICICI Life Insurance dropped 4%.
The new rules, if implemented, "substantially in the current form," could compress insurance distribution economics for banks and non-banking financial sector companies by 70%-90% in several high-margin categories, Citi said in a note.
The regulator has said the changes made in 2023 were "conceptually sound" but have "under-delivered on its objectives." It added that the removal of commission caps has increased commissions, especially among the private life and general insurers, as compared to state-backed sector insurers.
Long-term promise
India's insurance market holds long-term promise because only 3.7% of people have an insurance policy, compared to the global average of 7.3%, Mohammad Hassan, head of APAC equities dividend forecasting at S&P Global Market Intelligence, told CNBC. As a result, foreign insurance companies have been keen to enter and expand their presence in the market, he said.
In May, U.K.-based Prudential acquired a 75% stake in India's Bharti Life Insurance, while a month later, Aviva acquired the remaining 25% stake.
According to local media reports, several other global insurance companies such as AXA, Chubb, Allianz, and Old Mutual have also been looking to invest in the country's insurance sector.
With hard caps set on distribution commissions, it could be a challenge for insurance companies to grow. Distribution channels play a crucial role in selling financial products such as insurance, which are seen as push products, but their commission has been an issue of contention with regulators across several countries.
Chubb and Axa did not respond to CNBC's request for comments.
The insurance sector is now grappling with the "blanket-capping" introduced by the regulator that does not consider different gestation periods and complexities of products, Subramanian said.
As per IRDAI's annual report for the year ended March 2025, India's insurance penetration remained at 3.7%, unchanged from a year ago, as its life insurance penetration declined from 2.8% to 2.7% and non-life penetration remained at 1%.
The regulator expects the latest regulations to help companies improve the reach of insurance products. But the Insurance Brokers Association of India has warned that "commission caps below the cost of servicing customers could make it difficult for insurers and intermediaries to reach customers in smaller towns and cities," as per local media reports.
If the regulator's latest move manages to make insurance products more appetizing to customers — even as it crimps distributors' margins — it could be a "net-positive" for foreign insurers. But for now, they exacerbate the operational challenges, especially for global insurers in a market where price points are already much lower than most mature markets, experts said.
Need to know
India's viral Cockroach Party calls election panel head 'biggest threat' to democracy
Cockroach Janta Party, the viral pseudo-political movement behind the Gen Z protests that rattled Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government in July, has demanded the resignation of India's chief election officer after claiming he had undermined the country's democracy.
India readies $25 billion for Deep Tech investment as U.S. and China race ahead
India is preparing to deploy $25 billion to support Deep Tech start-ups in the country, as it tries to catch up with the U.S. and China in the global tech race to cut its reliance on frontier foreign technology.
Indian AI firm backed by Dune and Odyssey visual effects studio valued at $2 billion in fundraise
Brahma AI, an Indian start-up that makes artificial intelligence-generated audiovisual content for enterprise customers, has raised $150 million from a local private equity firm at a valuation of $2 billion.
Coming up
Oct. 6: India HSBC composite final PMI for September
Oct. 7: Reserve Bank of India policy meeting

articles.title: We're raising our Micron price target after an incredible quarter and robust guidance
articles.text: Micron on Wednesday evening delivered a much better-than-expected quarter and indicated that its fiscal year 2027 will be another strong one as demand for its memory products continues to exceed supply. Revenue in the fiscal 2026 fourth quarter, which ended Sept. 3, rose 379% year-over-year to $54.23 billion, a beat versus the $51.07 billion consensus forecast, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) increased 1,002% to $33.42, beating expectations of $31.61, LSEG data showed. MU YTD mountain Micron YTD Shares traded in a tight range in after-hours trading, but settled around the flat line after management finished its post-earnings conference call. The stock had a good September, rallying roughly 11%. For the year, Micron is up roughly 275%. However, it is down 12% from its record close of $,1213 on June 25. Bottom line It was a record-setting year for Micron as tight supply conditions and surging demand for memory in AI applications led to healthy increases in its average selling prices, resulting in soaring revenue, gross margins, and EPS. Remember, there are two main products in the memory market. There is NAND, which is storage memory, like a flash drive. There is also dynamic random access memory, or DRAM for short, which is considered working memory, like the RAM in your computer. There's also a specialized form of DRAM called HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, which is the key enabling technology for modern AI workloads. While AI accelerators do the math that underpins AI computing, they rely on HBM to store and feed them data. For AI to be deployed efficiently and at scale, systems require higher memory bandwidth and greater memory capacity. Due to the growing memory needs of AI systems, DRAM and NAND industry demand has significantly exceeded supply, and no one truly knows when the two will find a balance. As tight as memory and storage supply and demand conditions were in 2026, Micron expects conditions to be even tighter in calendar 2027 and 2028 because supply simply can't catch up to demand. Roughly 75% of Micron's expected output in 2027 is already spoken for, and customers are already speaking with the company on their allocations for 2028. "The structural gap between DRAM supply and demand growth rates is resulting in ongoing supply tightness, and cleanroom additions are required to augment node-transition supply growth and help narrow the gap," CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said in the company's prepared remarks. Cleanroom additions refer to the physical expansion of manufacturing capacity by building and installing more equipment. Jim Cramer recently visited one of the company's massive semiconductor fabrication sites, or fabs as the industry calls them, which is under construction near headquarters in Boise, Idaho. "Even with additional industry DRAM cleanroom space plans, with robust demand trends including new upside requests from customers, we do not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance," Mehrotra added. Demand for memory has fundamentally changed in this superintelligence era, and products from the three main players, U.S.-based Micron, as well as South Korean companies Samsung and SK Hynix , have become increasingly differentiated. While we should still think of memory as a cyclical industry where prices peak and decline as demand is overestimated and supply catches up, fears of peak pricing are why Micron trades at an incredibly cheap price-to-earnings multiple of around 6 times forward EPS estimates. This ongoing imbalance is driving price increases each quarter and causing customers to race to secure access to memory chips. Micron is signing more and more strategic customer agreements, or SCAs, to change its business model and provide greater visibility into future revenue and pricing. The goal of these SCAs is to move away from memory's boom-bust characterization and create a cycle that stays higher for longer, with more defined pricing bands. Micron has now signed up 26 SCAs to date, up from 16 last quarter. Typically, these agreements were supposed to last from calendar 2026 through the end of calendar 2030. However, Micron said more customers want to secure supply beyond that date, and the company is meeting those requests by signing one-year extensions to 2031. To help meet these customer agreements, Micron is committed to increasing capital expenditures to build new fabs and boost production. There is always risk when a company plans major capacity expansion programs because of shortages and price increases. In any cycle, the industry reaches a point where adding new capacity stokes fear of overbuilding, which would cause prices to plummet. However, Micron believes the revenue visibility the SCAs offer, as well as the cash deposits required in these deals, give them confidence to keep investing to meet soaring demand. There was nothing new in terms of a share repurchase program, but we still think a big one could be announced later this year. Micron has been prohibited from buying back stock beyond offsetting stock-based compensation due to a CHIPS Act funding agreement. Those restrictions are set to ease in December. With free cash flow of $33 billion in this quarter alone and an additional $128 billion expected to be generated in the new fiscal year, according to FactSet, Micron could potentially announce a share repurchase program that could rival Nvidia's recent record-setting $150 billion increase to its previously authorized $85 billion program. The market is currently treating Micron's beat and upside guidance as a good enough outcome to support the stock's recent rally. Micron can be volatile after earnings, so we'll wait and see where the chips fall Thursday morning. But with industry conditions in 2027 and 2028 expected to be even tighter than in 2026, Micron's earnings should continue to grow, while a massive buyback program could provide further support for the stock. We are increasing our price target to $1,200 from $1,100. We are also reiterating our buy-equivalent 1 rating, which is consistent with our most recent addition to the position on Sept. 3. Why we own it Micron should continue to benefit from the growing memory demands of AI, which are driving supply shortages and higher average selling prices. Newly signed strategic customer agreements (SCAs) should make earnings more durable than in past memory cycles, while growing free cash flow provides significant capacity for future share buybacks. Competitors: Samsung, SK Hynix Last buy: Sept. 3, 2026 Initiation date: Aug, 11, 2026 Outlook Turning to the guide, Micron expects revenue in its fiscal 2027 first quarter to be $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion. That's stronger than the $57.02 billion consensus estimate, according to LSEG. Over the full year, the company anticipates sequential revenue growth each quarter. Gross margin in the current quarter is expected to be approximately 86.25%, which is a slight dip from the Q4 result of 87% and slightly below estimates of 86.31%, according to FactSet. While that may be a little disappointing, the dip is mostly tied to the company's decision to increase compensation for its employees. That's an important distinction because a dip tied to softening average selling prices would be more worrisome. Easing any concerns around the gross margin decline, management said it believes fiscal Q1 will be the floor for gross margins for the year. Finally, off the strong revenue forecast, adjusted EPS is expected to be $38.15, plus or minus $1, which is above the consensus estimate of $35.40, according to LSEG. articles.title: OpenAI links China’s Moonshot AI to attempt to extract its models’ reasoning
articles.text:
OpenAI said it identified and disrupted a coordinated campaign in which operators attempted to extract protected reasoning from its artificial intelligence models, linking a core cluster of the activity with Chinese startup Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi.
The activity began in early July and later surged to 16,000 requests from more than 4,000 users over two days, OpenAI said. The company ultimately identified related activity across a cluster of more than 15,000 users and said it had fully disrupted the campaign by July 28.
The findings come just weeks after OpenAI rival Anthropic accused several Chinese AI developers, including Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of secretly using its Claude model to help train their own AI systems, underscoring growing concerns among U.S. AI companies that rivals could use their models to develop competing technology more quickly and cheaply.
OpenAI described the latest activity as "adversarial distillation," where one AI model's outputs or reasoning are used to help train or improve another model. The company said extracting such reasoning could allow others to reproduce advanced capabilities without making the same investment in developing and safeguarding frontier models, posing potential safety and national security risks.
The operators did not breach OpenAI's encryption, databases or stored user conversations, according to the company. Instead, they manipulated interactions with its models in an effort to reproduce hidden reasoning in a form visible to the requester.
OpenAI said it was unclear whether all the operators involved were linked to a single actor, but attributed a core cluster of the activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI. The company said it has shared its findings with other AI developers through the Frontier Model Forum as well as government information-sharing channels.
Moonshot did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

articles.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom bans AI 'robo bosses' in landmark state law, reversing his earlier veto
articles.text:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a landmark AI law banning Golden State employers from relying solely on artificial intelligence to fire or discipline workers.
SB 947, dubbed the No Robo Bosses Act, prevents businesses around the state from exclusively using "automated decision-making systems" in matters of employee discipline and termination. It also restricts their capacity to use AI as a principal tool in such decisions.
Under the bill, employers that rely "primarily" on AI output to make termination or disciplinary decisions must now have a human reviewer corroborate those decisions using additional information, such as managerial evaluations, peer reviews, and personnel files. Additionally, affected employees must be provided with written notice that AI was "primarily used" in their termination or disciplinary decision, a description of the employee data used by the system, and a human point of contact who can further explain the decision.
"No worker should ever be fired or disciplined by a machine, AI or not. Artificial intelligence systems have the potential to boost productivity, but they've also made errors and misjudgments and exhibited bias," California State Senator Jerry McNerney, the bill's author, told CNBC. "AI must remain a tool controlled by humans, not the other way around."
McNerney, a Democrat, first introduced the act in 2025, following a concerted push by organized labor in the state to erect guardrails around management's ability to use AI in taking adverse action against workers.
"When working people organize, we get results. Workers across California have demanded that our state lead the way in regulating AI in our workplaces. And today, we see that begin to happen," said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO and lead sponsor of No Robo Bosses Act, in a statement after Newsom signed it. "Today, California's workers and our unions have changed the national narrative on how Americans can fight back and win against AI taking over our jobs and workplaces."
Newsom has taken a flurry of recent actions on AI, including signing a broader executive order earlier this month addressing the potential existential risks posed by AI models "before it's too late," and a measure to provide a state framework for independent evaluation and auditing of AI models. Newsom said of the broad EO that the federal government was abdicating "its responsibility to protect Americans."
The U.S. is leading the way globally in adoption of automated management software and systems, according to survey results from the OECD published late last year. It found that algorithmic management software is being widely adopted across countries, but nowhere as widely as in the U.S., where 90% of managers say their firms have adopted at least one tool to "instruct, monitor or evaluate workers."
Meta is facing a lawsuit, filed in July, in which former employees allege AI-assisted systems were used to rank and select workers for layoffs, disproportionately affecting employees who had taken medical or family leave. Meta has denied the allegations.
Walmart and Amazon workers are increasingly concerned that HR decisions are being automated, according to a May survey released by nonprofit United for Respect, which has its roots in the labor movement and retail sector specifically. The nonprofit failed in an effort last summer to convince Walmart shareholders to approve a measure requiring company management to disclose more on use of AI with the workforce.
California's No Robo Bosses Act saw its momentum hit a wall in October when Newsom vetoed it despite clearing both of the state's legislative chambers with overwhelming majority support. Among his concerns, Newsom cited a requirement that would have compelled businesses to alert workers in advance whenever an AI system was in use that could affect work conditions.
"I share the author's concern that in certain cases unregulated use of ADS [automated decision-making software] by employers can be harmful to workers," the governor noted in his explanation, previewing future willingness to accept similar legislation. "However," he continued, "rather than addressing the specific ways employers misuse this technology, the bill imposes unfocused notification requirements on any business using even the most innocuous tools."
Upon re-introducing the bill in February after Newsom's resistance, McNerney removed the pre-notification requirement and stripped language that would have extended the Act's protections to gig workers, which had drawn heavy criticism from rideshare giants such as Uber and Lyft. Although these modifications have somewhat blunted the fierce lobbying efforts by tech and commerce groups that played a role in dooming the act's 2025 counterpart, California business leaders still rallied against SB 947 in the weeks leading up to its enactment.
"The bill's obligations generally apply when an employer 'primarily relies' on an automated decision system, but that critical term is never defined. Employers are given no objective standard for determining when a technology has moved from merely informing a decision to being a primary basis for it," Robert Singleton, the Chamber of Progress' senior director of policy and public affairs for California and US West, wrote in a letter to Newsom earlier this month, urging the governor to veto the bill. "Uncertainty about whether ordinary tools qualify as regulated automated decision systems could discourage employers from using technologies that improve consistency, identify safety risks, or help managers make better-informed decisions," he added.
First such law in nation as public turns on AI ahead of elections
While the aforementioned changes were made specifically to gain Newsom's approval, No Robo Bosses backers also benefitted from the fact that, this time around, the bill hit the governor's desk amidst all-time high public distrust surrounding AI's introduction and continued presence in the workplace. A July Gallup poll found that 39% of Americans believe that AI does more harm than good, an 8% increase from the 31% who felt similarly in 2025. Pew Research, in a study released this past August, similarly found that 71% of Americans think AI will "take people's jobs," an increase of around 7% from around two years ago.
This trend has solidified as Newsom weighs running for president in 2028, an election in which AI policy is expected to be a hot-button issue, particularly among Democratic hopefuls. But Democrats aren't alone on the issue. Earlier this month, Steve Hilton, California's Republican nominee for governor, came out in full support of the No Robo Bosses Act.
"The California Chamber…says rules requiring human review and basic accountability are too burdensome for employers. What a ridiculous thing for them to say," Hilton wrote in an open letter to Gonzalez. "In some ways, I don't think SB 947 goes far enough," he wrote. "Employers should not be allowed to use AI to decide whether someone is fired, demoted, loses regular hours, or is shut out of the program they rely on for income."
California businesses will be the first to navigate its distinct regulatory framework, which establishes a largely unprecedented level of oversight over workplace AI use. Some local regulations throughout the past five years have imposed restrictions on how AI can be used in employment decisions, perhaps most notably Illinois' Public Act 103-0804, which also requires employers to notify workers when they use AI for a set of specified employment purposes. However, these restrictions have never gone to the lengths now seen under California law. Even the Illinois law, which went into effect this past January, stops short of an outright prohibition on deploying agentic digital systems for employment decisions.
While the No Robo Bosses Act is the first of its kind to become law, many other bills currently sit in limbo across the nation, designed to fulfill the very same purpose. This past June, U.S. Senators Ed Markey (D.-Mass.) and Brian Schatz (D.-Hawaii), both Democrats, introduced federal legislation donning the same name, which would bar employers from "relying on automated decision systems to make work-related decisions." Markey's bill, presented to a Congress that has been slow to develop any sort of legislation regulating AI, was effectively dead on arrival. A number of states, including New York, Louisiana, and New Jersey, have seen similar legislation be proposed but have yet to act on their own accord.
Earlier this year, New York became the first state in the nation to enact a ban on the construction of new AI data centers.
California's action may have just provided the push other states need to move on workplace AI legislation.
Left-leaning civil liberties nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation said in a statement to CNBC that signing the law is a "strong step toward giving workers the protections they need in workplaces that use automated decisionmaking systems" and it planned to continue its work with labor groups to "advance policies that protect human dignity in the workplace."

articles.title: Where Cramer stands on a buzzy behind-the-meter name powering the AI build-out
articles.text:
After an enormous run this year, Cramer said Wednesday that he would wait for a pullback in this name.
He said it is his favorite way to gain exposure to behind-the-meter electricity powering the AI build-out.
CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday that Bloom Energy remains his favorite way to invest in behind-the-meter electricity powering the artificial intelligence build-out. He's just not ready to pull the trigger just yet. Bloom shares have surged 219% this year, including 34% this month, as demand for its onsite fuel-cell systems has accelerated alongside the construction of power-hungry AI data centers. These scalable modular blocks, which can provide primary and backup power outside of the public electrical grid, convert fuel into electricity without combustion. The stock has nearly doubled since Cramer covered it in February . "If you want exposure to the electricity powering the AI build-out, Bloom Energy remains my favorite way to play it," the " Mad Money " host said. "Long term, I think this one can still go much higher over the next few years." Bloom's technology offers data center developers a faster alternative to waiting years for a power grid connection. Management said it was able to deliver power to an Oracle data center within 55 days. Data center size is measured in the gigawatts of continuous power needed to run the facilities because energy is the limiting factor on capacity. Demand has already shown in Bloom's results. Second-quarter revenue jumped 166% to $1.07 billion, crushing estimates, while adjusted earnings of 78 cents per share nearly doubled expectations. Management also raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $3.9 billion and $4.2 billion, with the midpoint implying sales will double. Bloom is set to report third-quarter results Oct. 27. Cramer also pointed to Bloom's expanding customer base. The company said that buy-in from major hyperscalers, more than a dozen neoclouds, and AI labs have validated the technology. Bloom competes with other ways of generating behind-the-meter power, like the massive jet-engine-like turbines from GE Vernova , a holding in the CNBC Investing Club portfolio . As much as Cramer likes the Bloom story, he said investors shouldn't chase it. Bloom trades at roughly 108 times this year's expected earnings-per-share and 59 times next year's EPS estimates. "Wait for a pullback, because we're going to get one, and it'll be another gift for long-term investors," he concluded. articles.title: Cramer says 'frozen' conditions are holding many stocks back. Here's what could change that
articles.text:
CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday that investors shouldn't jump ship despite signs of slowing activity across key parts of the economy.
Cramer's comments come as high interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty and political opposition weigh on stocks across industries. The U.S. housing market remains mired in a multiyear period of sluggishness, IPO and M&A activity has slowed, and even the booming data-center buildout is facing new obstacles — leaving fewer catalysts to drive crucial parts of the market higher.
"Market after market is getting frozen right now and that's killing stocks," the "Mad Money" host said.
Housing is perhaps the clearest example. The 30-year mortgage rate has climbed to roughly 7.5%, from about 3% five years ago, leaving many homeowners locked into cheaper mortgages reluctant or unable to move.
"The nearly 7.5% mortgage has made housing the least affordable it's been in 40 years," Cramer said.
The slowdown has rippled across housing-related stocks, including homebuilders Lennar and KB Home and retailers Home Depot and Lowe's, both of which hit fresh 52-week lows on Wednesday. Fewer home sales also mean less spending on appliances, furniture and renovations, pressuring stocks like Whirlpool, which also hit a 52-week low Wednesday. Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by the CNBC Investing Club, owns shares of Home Depot.
Once-booming capital markets are also showing signs of slowing. Cramer pointed to smart ring maker Oura's decision to postpone its planned $2.2 billion IPO, as well as Dunkin Donuts and Buffalo Wild Wings' parent Inspire Brands shelving its own offering.
Shares of Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs — the premier investment banks on Wall Street — both declined roughly 12% in the month of September and set their highs for the year in July. The Investing Club owns Goldman shares.
"Without IPOs or M&A, the huge banking cohort is frozen except for fees," Cramer said. "That's just not good enough."
Even the booming data-center industry faces new obstacles as political concerns around electricity costs and other impacts threaten to slow development. The stakes are raised by this being a midterm election year, with Democrats and Republicans vying for control of Congress.
But Cramer cautioned investors against abandoning the market because headwinds can quickly turn into tailwinds. Most notably, an end to the war could push oil and inflation lower, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to take another interest rate hike off the table and unleashing a powerful stock rally.
"It could happen in three quick days, perhaps the three most important days of 2026," Cramer said. "That's why I hesitate to leave the market at this moment."
If the economy starts to thaw, Cramer concluded, "then you get a virtual running of the bulls."

articles.text:
MPLX LP: "It's a stock that yields 7.6% and it can cover that dividend and then some. That's the kind of thing I'm looking for: an oil play that gives you a good yield."
Grail: "I've been waiting for that approval, and I said, 'if it happens, this thing is going to spike.' I don't think it's done yet. I think it's like Moderna when it was like at $120. I think this thing can go higher."
